info.title: Heyarr
info.summary: Headless content lifecycle, replication and consumption for homelabs.
info.description:
Every error is an RFC 9457 problem document with a stable `type` URI. Clients
branch on `type` — not on the title, not on the detail, and not on the HTTP
status alone, which several different conditions share.

Collections are paginated by keyset with an opaque cursor. `next_cursor` is
absent on the last page, so "keep going while next_cursor is set" is the
whole client loop. The cursor's contents are not a contract: it encodes the
sort key of the last row returned, and a client that parses it breaks the
first time a sort order changes.

tags.name: content
tags.description: Works, editions, assets and the libraries they come from.

tags.name: bytes
tags.description: Blob metadata. The bytes themselves are a separate contract (ADR-0013).

tags.name: operations
tags.description: Jobs, events, credentials and system state.

tags.name: policy
tags.description: Quality profiles — the standard desired state is measured against (§62).

tags.name: desired
tags.description: What should exist, whether or not it does yet (§55).

tags.name: providers
tags.description: The centralised registry of external services — indexers, download clients (§59).

tags.name: mcp
tags.description: Semantic actions for agents, over JSON-RPC (§71, ADR-0019).

tags.name: peer
tags.description:
The inter-peer surface. A SEPARATE listener with a separate credential:
mutual TLS pinned to peer membership (§26, ADR-0012). No bearer token is
accepted here and no peer certificate authenticates anything under
/api/v1.

tags.name: personal-state
tags.description:
Encrypted personal state (§38, §42, ADR-0049). A device pushes opaque
spaces, wrapped keys and ciphertext changes; the server stores them and
can read none of it. Fetching ciphertext needs `read`; storing it needs
`write`; a wrapped key no token conveys is what turns ciphertext into
plaintext, and only on an authorised device (Invariant 6).

tags.name: compat
tags.description:
Compatibility adapters that let existing client ecosystems talk to Heyarr
over their own protocols (§70), as read-only projections over the
canonical model. OpenSubsonic for music is the first. Mounted outside
/api/v1 with the protocol's own authentication, and exposing no personal
state (§72).

get.summary: Liveness.
get.description:
This process is running and its HTTP stack works. It checks nothing else
on purpose: a liveness probe that fails because the database is busy
causes a restart loop that makes the database busier.

get.summary: Readiness.
get.description:
Whether this process can actually serve requests. Deliberately free of
anything an unauthenticated caller should not learn — no paths, no
versions, no counts.

503.description: Not ready.

get.summary: Prometheus metrics.
get.description:
Authenticated exactly like the API and requiring `read`. Route names,
library sizes and request patterns are not "just metrics".

200.description: Metrics in the Prometheus text exposition format.

get.summary: What this node is, what it is running, and how far that has drifted.
get.description:
The `drift` object answers "how far behind is this instance", and it
answers with a distance rather than a boolean. A deployment once ran 36
commits and seven unapplied migrations behind `main`, across two whole
milestones, and nothing reported it — every input to the check already
existed and nothing compared them.

The SCHEMA half needs nothing from the caller: a binary embeds its own
migrations, so it already knows the highest version that exists and can
compare that against what is applied. Pass `expected_schema` to compare
against something else instead.

The BUILD half cannot be answered alone — a binary has no idea what
release was supposed to be deployed — so the expectation is supplied per
request. Without it the build half reports `unknown`, which is
deliberately not `current`: a check that has quietly stopped comparing
must not look like a fleet that never drifts.

parameters.name: expected_version
parameters.description:
The version this instance was expected to be running, e.g. `v1.4.0`.
Ordering is by semantic version when both sides carry one; otherwise
`expected_commit` decides whether the builds are the same build.

parameters.name: expected_commit
parameters.description:
The commit this instance was expected to be built from. Matched by
prefix, with a floor of seven characters, so an abbreviated stamp
still matches its full form.

parameters.name: expected_schema
parameters.description:
The schema version its database was expected to be at. Defaults to
the highest migration THIS binary embeds. A value that is not a
non-negative integer is rejected rather than ignored: falling back
to the default would answer a question nobody asked and report
`current` for it.

get.summary: Page the catalog.
get.description:
Ordered by `(sort_title, id)`. The id is in the sort key because
sort_title is not unique, and a non-unique keyset boundary skips and
repeats rows exactly as OFFSET does.

parameters.name: content_type
parameters.description: Restrict to one content type.

parameters.name: library_id
parameters.description: Works with at least one asset in this library.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Case-insensitive substring match over `sort_title`.

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description:
`title` is `(sort_title, id)` ascending. `recent` is
`(created_at, id)` descending — the "recently added" shelf
(ADR-0075). Each order has its own cursor: a cursor from one is
refused by the other rather than read as a position in a
different order.

parameters.name: year
parameters.description: Exactly this year.

parameters.name: year_from
parameters.description: This year or later.

parameters.name: year_to
parameters.description: This year or earlier.

parameters.name: artist
parameters.description:
Works whose `attributes.artist` is exactly this — an artist's
albums, keyed by the name `GET /artists` reports (ADR-0075).

parameters.name: author
parameters.description:
Works whose `attributes.author` is exactly this — an author's
books, keyed by the name `GET /authors` reports (ADR-0075).

parameters.name: include
parameters.description:
Comma-separated browse embeds to add to each row (ADR-0075):
`artwork` (the poster) and `primary_asset` (the file a tap plays).
An embed not asked for is absent; one asked for that the work
lacks is `null`. With no `include` the rows are plain `Work`s. An
unknown name is a 400.

200.description: A page of works — plain, or cards when `include` was given.

get.summary: A work's poster, by redirect to its blob.
get.description:
Answers `307` with a `Location` of the ordinary blob route for the
work's representative artwork asset (ADR-0075) — a `poster`/`cover`
before an unnamed image before `fanart`/`backdrop`/`banner`, the id
breaking ties, and only an asset that holds bytes and is not missing.

A redirect rather than a second byte route on purpose: the blob route
is the one contract for bytes (ADR-0013), and its immutable cache
headers are correct only because the URL is the hash. A work's poster
can change, so this work-keyed URL carries a short private `max-age`
and the target carries the immutable one. `307`, not `302`, so a
`HEAD` stays a `HEAD`.

No resizing: the node has no image library and no thumbnail cache. A
client that already holds the `artwork` embed can skip this route and
fetch `artwork.content_url` directly.

The guest boundary applies (ADR-0074): a `vault` poster is a 404 to a
Guest, as the asset itself is.

404.description: No such work, or the work has no artwork (the detail says which).

head.description: Identical to `get`: a `307` with the same `Location`, so a client can learn whether a poster exists without following the redirect. A 307 preserves the method, which is why the redirect is not a 302.

404.description: No such work

get.summary: Page the artists — a grouping over music works.
get.description:
An artist is not an entity (ADR-0075): it is the distinct
`attributes.artist` the music identifier wrote, with how many works
carry it and the cover of the first of them (by year, then title) as
its picture. An artist's albums are
`GET /works?content_type=music&artist=<name>&include=artwork,primary_asset`.

Ordered by name (case-insensitively), under its own cursor. A name is
exact: the day a metadata provider supplies artist identifiers, an
artist entity that merges spellings is justified — not before.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Case-insensitive substring match over the name.

get.summary: Page the authors — a grouping over book works.
get.description:
The book-shaped sibling of `GET /artists` (ADR-0075): the distinct
`attributes.author`, a count, and the cover of the first book. An
author's books are `GET /works?content_type=book&author=<name>`.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Case-insensitive substring match over the name.

get.summary: One work, with its external identifiers.

patch.description:
Changes the title, year or content type (#428). Every field is optional;
omitting one leaves it alone, and `"year": 0` clears the year — the two
are different requests.

**`work_key` is deliberately not recomputed.** It is the normalised
identity a rescan converges on, derived from the title a SCANNER sees,
not from the one a person prefers to read. Re-deriving it on a rename
would make the next scan create a second work instead of finding this
one. `sort_title` does follow the title, because it is the listing's
sort key.

The title is stored as typed, not passed through the scanner's display
normaliser — that normaliser would read "(Extended)" as a release tag
and drop it.

delete.summary: Remove a work, its editions, its assets and its wants.
delete.description:
**Logical, in ADR-0018's sense: no byte is unlinked.** The catalog rows
go — the work, its editions, the asset rows beneath them, and every want
anchored to it — and the blobs stay. The existing `gc_blobs` sweeper
reclaims a blob no asset references any more, behind its grace window.
The emitted events say `bytes_removed: false` in as many words.

**Wants are cascade-cancelled; a followed source refuses the delete.**
A want is a one-off intent that deleting its target supersedes. A
followed source is standing configuration that will keep producing
wants, so a work that is still followed answers `409` naming the fix
(`DELETE /followed-sources/{id}`, which also decides what happens to the
archive) rather than silently dropping the subscription.

Emits `content.asset.deleted` per removed asset — the same type and
payload the per-asset route emits, so a subscriber need not special-case
"unless the whole work went" — a `desired.removed` per cancelled want,
and one `content.work.deleted`.

get.summary: The files belonging to one work.
get.description:
Joined through the work's editions, with the edition label and the
blob's size and media type inlined — the two extra reads a work-detail
screen would otherwise make per asset (#429).

An unknown work is a 404, never an empty page: "this work has no files"
and "there is no such work" are different answers.

parameters.name: state
parameters.description: The same filter `GET /assets` takes.

200.description: A page of the work's files.

get.summary: One edition, with its external identifiers.

delete.summary: Remove an edition, its assets, its items and its wants. Requires `write`.
delete.description:
**Logical, in ADR-0018's sense: no byte is unlinked.** The catalog rows
go — the edition, the asset rows beneath it, its byte-less items and the
wants scoped to it — and the blobs stay. The parent work is untouched: an
edition is a subordinate, scanner-recreatable grouping, so a rescan
re-derives it from the files that remain. The existing `gc_blobs` sweeper
reclaims a blob no asset references any more, behind its grace window.
The emitted events say `bytes_removed: false` in as many words.

**Wants are cascade-cancelled; a followed work refuses the delete.** A
want scoped to the edition (or to one of its items) is a one-off intent
that removing its target supersedes. A follow source is standing
configuration anchored to the WORK that keeps projecting its items — its
seasons are exactly these editions — so an edition whose work is still
followed answers `409` naming the fix (`DELETE /followed-sources/{id}`,
which also decides what happens to the archive) rather than letting the
next poll silently re-materialise what was just removed.

Emits `content.asset.deleted` per removed asset — the same type and
payload the per-asset route emits, so a subscriber need not special-case
"unless the whole edition went" — a `desired.removed` per cancelled want,
and one `content.edition.deleted`.

get.summary: Page the files.

parameters.name: state
parameters.description:
`missing` is an asset whose source path has vanished. It is not a
deletion: the catalog row and any blob both remain (ADR-0018).

get.summary: One asset.

delete.description:
Logical, per ADR-0018. The asset stops existing; its blob does not. A
later `gc_blobs` sweep reclaims blobs that no asset references, once a
grace window has passed — which is what makes a mistaken delete
reversible. Nothing is unlinked inside this request.

get.summary: Page the libraries, each with its roots.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Case-insensitive substring match over the name.

post.summary: Create a library. Requires `write`.

get.summary: The encrypted spaces this peer holds — metadata only (§38).
get.description:
Returns each space's opaque id, structural kind and when the peer
recorded it. There is no name, no member list and no key: those are
encrypted state, never metadata a peer stores.

200.description: The spaces this peer holds (possibly empty).

post.summary: Record a client-minted space and the wrapped copies of its key. Requires `write`.
post.description:
The device mints the space id and space key together and seals the key
for each recipient client-side; this stores the opaque space and the
wrapped copies. The server holds a key it cannot open (ADR-0049).

id.description: The client-minted opaque space id (a UUIDv7).

get.summary: The wrapped copies of a space's key — a device finds the one sealed for it.
get.description:
Each entry names the recipient key the copy was sealed for and the
opaque wrapped bytes. The peer holds these and no private key, so it
cannot open any of them (Invariant 6).

200.description: The wrapped keys for the space (possibly empty).

post.summary: Re-wrap a space's key for the remaining recipients after a rotation. Requires `write`.
post.description:
Replaces the wrapped copies of a space's key — the remaining recipients'
copies now seal the NEW key minted by a rotation (§41, #361). Each copy is
opaque; the peer upserts it and opens none. The revoked recipient's copy is
deleted separately via DELETE /spaces/{id}/keys/{recipient}.

200.description: How many recipient copies were replaced.

delete.summary: Delete one recipient's wrapped copy of a space's key — revocation. Requires `admin`.
delete.description:
Deletes the wrapped copy sealed for one recipient (§41, ADR-0049, #361).
After it, that recipient holds no copy of the key; combined with a rotation
that re-keys for everyone else, the revoked device can read nothing
encrypted from here on. Idempotent: deleting a copy already gone is a 204,
not a 404.

parameters.name: recipient
parameters.description: The recipient key id ("x25519:<hex>"), URL-escaped.

204.description: The wrapped copy is gone (or was already).

get.summary: A space's encrypted changes — ciphertext a device pulls to decrypt and merge (§42).
get.description:
Every change is opaque: a content-addressed id, its causal parents, and
ciphertext. The peer never decrypted any of it; the semantic merge is
client-side.

200.description: The changes the peer holds for the space (possibly empty).

post.summary: Store one encrypted change; the peer verifies its content-address. Requires `write`.
post.description:
The peer re-derives the change's blake3 id over its space, parents and
ciphertext and refuses a mismatch — it never trusts a claimed id
(Invariant 1). It stores the ciphertext without decrypting it.

201.description: The id the peer verified and stored the change under.

get.summary: The latest encrypted snapshot for a space — ciphertext (§44).
get.description:
Returns the most recent snapshot the peer holds — a materialised CRDT
state at a causal point, as ciphertext the peer never decrypted — so a
joining device syncs a bounded snapshot plus the tail rather than the
whole log. 404 when the space has no snapshot yet.

post.summary: Push a materialised, encrypted snapshot. Requires `write`.

201.description: The id the peer verified and stored the snapshot under.

post.summary: Drop the changes the latest snapshot subsumes and every replica holds. Requires `admin`.
post.description:
Compacts the change log: drops changes the latest snapshot subsumes and
that lie within the acknowledged frontier (the frontier every trusted Full
Peer holds), so a change a partitioned peer still needs survives (§44).

frontier.description: The acknowledged causal frontier every replica holds.

post.summary: Reconcile encrypted personal state to all trusted Full Peers now. Requires `admin`.
post.description:
Runs one on-demand reconcile: for every local space, push its metadata,
wrapped keys and the changes each Full Peer is missing, as ciphertext
(§37, §45). Leaderless and idempotent — a converged fleet is a no-op — and
an unreachable peer is recorded and retried next cycle, not an error.

200.description: How many (peer, space) pairs converged and how many were deferred.

503.description: This node replicates encrypted state to no peers.

get.summary: One library, with its roots.

delete.summary: Remove an empty library and its roots. Requires `write`.
delete.description:
Removes the library and its roots (`library_roots` is `ON DELETE
CASCADE`). The library must hold no assets: a library that still has
content is refused `409`, naming the fix (delete its works first via
`DELETE /api/v1/works/{id}`), because `assets.library_id` is `ON DELETE
SET NULL` and a raw delete would silently orphan a whole library's
content rather than refuse (#228, ADR-0083). Logical in ADR-0018's
sense: catalog rows go, bytes stay for the GC sweep.

post.summary: Add a root to a library. Requires `write`.

ingest_mode.description:
How ingest materialises bytes into the CAS (ADR-0014).
`link` catalogues files where they are and never copies them
(ADR-0020).

patch.summary: Change an existing root's ingest mode. Requires `write`.
patch.description:
Change how a root materialises ingested bytes without tearing it down
and rebuilding it (#222). The mode governs how the NEXT ingest
materialises, so blobs already in the store keep the inode they arrived
with — safe to run on a live root. The root is addressed under its own
library, so a root id belonging to another library is a `404`, never a
cross-library edit. The body must change something: an omitted
`ingest_mode` is a `400`, as is an empty or unknown one.

parameters.name: rootID
parameters.description: The root's id, as `library list` shows it.

ingest_mode.description:
How ingest materialises bytes into the CAS (ADR-0014).
`link` catalogues files where they are and never copies them
(ADR-0020).

delete.summary: Remove one root from a library. Requires `write`.
delete.description:
Heyarr stops scanning that directory. Always safe: an asset references
its library, never a root, so no ingested content is orphaned — only the
root's scanned-file records go with it (#228, ADR-0083). The root is
addressed under its own library, so a root id belonging to another
library is a `404`, never a cross-library delete.

parameters.name: rootID
parameters.description: The root's id, as `library list` shows it.

post.summary: Enqueue a scan. Requires `write`.
post.description:
One `scan_library` job per enabled root, because the scanner's job is
root-scoped. A library with two roots therefore yields two jobs, and a
client waiting on the scan must wait on all of them — waiting on the
first only is how a CLI exits 0 with half the library unscanned.

Enqueueing is idempotent while a scan of the same root is still live: a
second request returns the running job rather than queueing a second
walk of the same tree (ADR-0008).

409.description:
The library has no enabled roots, so there is nothing to scan.
Returning 202 here would let a client believe a scan is running.

get.summary: Blob metadata.
get.description:
Metadata only. The bytes are served by `/api/v1/blobs/{hash}/content`,
which is deliberately a separate contract with four consumers
(ADR-0013).

get.summary: List the renderers on this node's network (§68).
get.description:
Televisions, speakers and projectors that Heyarr can play to, found by SSDP on the local segment.

An empty list means nothing ANSWERED, not that nothing is there. A screen in standby closes every listener and on some models leaves the network entirely, so a device that is switched off is indistinguishable from one that does not exist. Discovery is also multicast, so it does not cross a routed link: a controller on the far side of a VPN finds nothing at all.

parameters.name: refresh
parameters.description: `true` searches again instead of reusing the cached sweep. A search takes several seconds, so this is for "I just switched it on".

parameters.name: udn
parameters.description: The renderer's UPnP UDN, from `GET /api/v1/renderers`.

get.summary: Report what a renderer is doing.
get.description: Transport state and, when the device reports one, position. A renderer that answers no position is not broken — `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` is a legal answer and some devices give it forever.

404.description: No renderer with that id answered.

parameters.name: udn
parameters.description: The renderer's UPnP UDN, from `GET /api/v1/renderers`.

post.summary: Plan a playback, mint a capability URL and push it to a renderer.
post.description:
One call, deliberately. Plan, mint and push always happen together, and a client made to orchestrate them is a client that can get the order wrong, hold a capability it never uses, or open a session for a playback it never started.

The renderer's own `GetProtocolInfo` answer becomes the Device profile the planner decides against, so the file is judged on what that television said about itself rather than on what somebody typed in.

409.description: Nothing to play from — most often a replica on another peer, since a capability is only valid at the peer that signed it (ADR-0040).

502.description: The renderer refused, with its own UPnP error. `714 Illegal MIME-type` and `701 Transition not available` are different problems and need different fixes, so the device's answer is passed through rather than flattened.

parameters.name: udn
parameters.description: The renderer's UPnP UDN, from `GET /api/v1/renderers`.

post.summary: Hold position.

parameters.name: udn
parameters.description: The renderer's UPnP UDN, from `GET /api/v1/renderers`.

post.summary: Continue from where it was paused.
post.description: This is UPnP's Play. There is no separate resume verb: Play from PAUSED_PLAYBACK continues, and Play from STOPPED restarts.

parameters.name: udn
parameters.description: The renderer's UPnP UDN, from `GET /api/v1/renderers`.

post.summary: End playback and release the content.

parameters.name: udn
parameters.description: The renderer's UPnP UDN, from `GET /api/v1/renderers`.

post.summary: Jump to a position.
post.description: `seconds` is an ABSOLUTE offset from the start, not a delta. It maps to UPnP's REL_TIME, which means the same thing despite its name.

parameters.name: capability
parameters.description: A signed, expiring, single-blob capability minted by `POST /api/v1/playback`. It IS the authority for this request — there is no other credential — so treat it as a secret.

get.summary: Serve one blob to a device that cannot present a credential.
get.description:
The renderer route of ADR-0040, and the only unauthenticated content path in Heyarr. It exists because a television, a speaker or a projector is handed a URL and told to fetch it: it cannot send an `Authorization` header, and `/api/v1/blobs/{hash}/content` therefore answers every such device with 401.

This is NOT a second way to read the library. The capability in the path names ONE blob and expires, so a leaked URL discloses one title for one window rather than everything. It is mounted outside `/api/v1` deliberately — inside it, the bearer requirement would 401 the very devices it exists for.

Bytes, ranges and validators are identical to the blob endpoint: this route wraps that handler rather than reimplementing it. The one difference is `Content-Type`, which is the Asset's declared media type rather than `application/octet-stream`, because a DLNA renderer refuses the latter. The type is signed into the capability, so it cannot be altered in transit.

A capability is only valid at the peer that signed it.

200.description: The whole blob, typed as the Asset says.

404.description: No content is available at this address. Every refusal is this response, byte for byte: an expired capability, one signed by another peer, a malformed one and a blob this peer does not hold are deliberately indistinguishable, so the route cannot be used as an oracle. The `instance` is a constant for the same reason — it would otherwise echo the capability back.

416.description: The requested range lies outside the blob.

head.summary: Report size and range support to a renderer before it fetches.
head.description: Identical to `get` in every header, with no body. Renderers routinely HEAD before they GET, and one that receives a 405 gives up without playing anything.

200.description: The blob exists; `Content-Length` is its size.

404.description: See `get`.

parameters.name: capability
parameters.description: As above.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: A cosmetic trailing filename, ignored entirely. Some renderers will not issue a GET for a URL whose last segment looks like nothing they recognise. It is outside the signature because it decides nothing: both the media type and the bytes come from the capability.

get.summary: As `/render/{capability}`, with a filename a renderer will accept.

404.description: See `/render/{capability}`.

head.summary: As `/render/{capability}`, with a filename a renderer will accept.

404.description: See `/render/{capability}`.

parameters.name: session
parameters.description: A rendezvous label the two devices agree on out of band (the old device generates it and shows it, in a QR or a short code, to the new one). It is NOT a secret — the pairing's security is the short authentication string the humans compare, not the obscurity of this id — and a URL-safe token of at most 128 characters.

parameters.name: slot
parameters.description: One of the fixed handshake slots: `initiator_commit`, `responder_commit`, `initiator_reveal`, `responder_reveal`, `cert` or `abort`. Any other name is a 400.

put.summary: Post one value into a pairing handshake slot (§40, ADR-0022, ADR-0038).
put.description:
The device-pairing relay, and — with `render` — one of Heyarr's two unauthenticated surfaces. It exists because enrolment is PAIRING, not sharing (ADR-0022): a new device that is not yet enrolled has no credential to present, and the old device authorises it directly, with the server acting only as a dumb store-and-forward.

Every value that crosses this relay is PUBLIC — a commitment (a hash), a public key, a session salt, or a signed enrolment cert — so a relay that read every byte would still learn nothing it could pair with (ADR-0038). The relay never joins two sessions, never inspects a value and vouches for nothing; the man-in-the-middle defence is the commit-before-reveal ordering and the short authentication string the two humans compare, neither of which this endpoint can see or affect.

Slots are write-once: a second PUT of the same bytes is idempotent, a different value to a written slot is a 409. Sessions are in-memory, bounded and short-lived (a ten-minute TTL, a per-slot size cap, a cap on live sessions), which is the whole security surface of serving this without a credential — it grants no authority, so the only abuse is memory, and the bounds close it.

204.description: The value was stored (or an identical value already was).

400.description: An unknown slot name or a malformed session id.

409.description: The slot already holds a different value; slots are write-once.

413.description: The value is larger than the per-slot cap.

429.description: Too many live pairing sessions; try again once some expire.

get.summary: Read one value from a pairing handshake slot.
get.description: The other half of the relay: the peer polls the slot it is waiting on until it appears. Returns the opaque bytes another device posted, or a 404 while the slot is still empty (which is the ordinary "keep waiting") or once the session has expired.

400.description: A malformed session id.

404.description: Nothing is stored at this slot yet, or the session has expired.

post.summary: A paired device enrols itself at this peer (ADR-0067, ADR-0068).
post.description:
The step after pairing. A device that holds its admitting membership op — a cert the user's genesis key signed for its key, or (ADR-0068) an `add` signed by any current member of the identity — presents that op and a fresh possession proof over it — the exact two halves of the `Device` credential — and is recorded under its pinned user, with no admin call to `/api/v1/identities/devices` in between.

It is public because the device may not yet be known here and so cannot authenticate; it grants nothing because the op, evaluated with the identity's op log (voidbind-go ADR-0007), already proves a member vouched for the device and the proof proves the caller holds the key. Verification is the same code the `Device` scheme runs on every request: the op's user must be PINNED here (ADR-0032's gate holds — an unknown user's op is refused), the possession proof must be signed by the op's device key over this op and be fresh, and the membership evaluated over the ops this node holds plus `ops` must admit the device. A device admitted by a member this node has never met MUST send that member's admission in `ops` (or the `Voidbind-Membership` header), or its own admission cites a past the node cannot judge. The enrolled device authenticates at the READ floor; write remains an admin authorisation of the device key (ADR-0065).

Under ADR-0068 the evaluation itself materialises the device's row (a member authenticates on first contact); what this route adds is the NAME and the created/existing answer. Idempotent on the device key: a re-submission returns the existing device with a 200. A REVOKED device is not re-enrolled, and an op naming a different user than the row holds is refused. Every refusal is the same opaque 401 the `Device` scheme returns; the reason is logged, not disclosed.

op.description: The device's admitting membership op token (a v3 `add`, or a v1/v2 cert — the same slot). Exactly one of `op` and `cert` is required; both is accepted when they are equal.

cert.description: The ADR-0067 spelling of `op`, kept for clients that send a user-signed cert; it carries a v3 op just as well.

proof.description: A fresh possession proof over the op (the value after the `~` in a `Device` credential): `{"v":2,"crt":base64url(sha256(op)),"iat","exp"}` signed by the device key, `exp - iat` of 120 seconds.

name.description: A display name for the device; defaults to `device`.

ops.description: Membership op tokens the device knows (ADR-0068), merged into the evaluation exactly as the `Voidbind-Membership` header is on an authenticated request. At most 64 in total across body and header.

200.description: The device was already enrolled; this is its existing record.

400.description: The body is not a single JSON object of the documented fields, is too large, or presents more than 64 ops.

401.description: The credential was rejected — for any reason (unpinned user, bad signature, expired add, an admission citing ops this node cannot see, a removed device, wrong or stale proof, revoked device). The detail is the same in every case.

parameters.name: usr
parameters.description: The identity — its genesis public key, `ed25519:<hex>`.

get.summary: The membership ops this node holds for an identity (ADR-0068).
get.description: Every membership op token (voidbind-go ADR-0007: `add` / `remove`, signed by a member or by the genesis key) this node has recorded for the identity, oldest issued first. A device merges them with its own and evaluates; the node does not pre-chew a view, because a view is a function of the ops and the reader's clock. This is how a device learns that a member removed it, or another device, while it was offline. Public: an op carries its own authority and the node adds none by serving it; the identity's genesis key is not guessable, so there is nothing to enumerate.

400.description: `usr` is not a rendered Ed25519 public key.

404.description: No such identity is pinned here.

post.summary: Push membership ops to this node (ADR-0068).
post.description: Records ops a device signed or learned — a `remove`, typically — so the node evaluates them from now on. The ops are evaluated merged with the log first and recorded only if EVERY one is structurally valid for this identity (parses, verifies under its signer, names this identity, cites ops the node can see): junk anywhere in the body is one opaque 401 and nothing is written. A valid but ineffective op (an unauthorised signer, an outranked remove, a re-add of a removed device) IS recorded — it is part of the state — and evaluation is what decides it changes nothing. Idempotent by op hash. A device the evaluation removes is tombstoned in the node's view at once, exactly as an admin revocation is.

200.description: The ops were evaluated and the new ones recorded; the whole log follows.

400.description: The body is not a single JSON object of the documented fields, is too large, has no ops, or has more than 64; or `usr` is not a key.

401.description: At least one op was rejected. The detail is the same in every case; the reason is logged.

404.description: No such identity is pinned here.

post.summary: Open a Voidbind pairing session (ADR-0066).
post.description:
The Voidbind relay — voidbind-go's `relay` protocol, which the `voidbind` CLI (`pair-initiate` / `pair-join`) and the phone client speak — mounted beside the legacy `/pair` relay so this node can be the rendezvous for its own devices. A Voidbind client is pointed at `<node>/pair` as its relay BASE (the client appends `/v1/...` itself, exactly as against a standalone `voidbind relay`) and lands here.

Like `/pair` it is public and grants nothing: an in-memory, write-once, opaque blob store addressed by (session, role, type) that never parses a payload and holds no key. What crosses it is either public (two commitments, two revealed public keys) or ciphertext it cannot open (the enrolment cert, sealed to the new device's X25519 key). The initiator — the machine holding the user identity — opens the session and shares its id and a salt with the new device out of band (the invite QR).

session_id.description: The rendezvous label both devices dial; not a secret.

503.description: Too many live sessions; try again once some expire.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: The session id returned when the session was opened.

parameters.name: role
parameters.description: Whose slot: `initiator` (the existing, authorising device) or `responder` (the new device). Each role writes only its own slots and reads only the peer's.

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: The message slot: `commit` (a commitment over the keys about to be revealed), `reveal` (the revealed public keys, JSON), or `cert` (the sealed enrolment cert, initiator only).

put.summary: Store one role's message in a Voidbind pairing session (ADR-0066).
put.description: Write-once: a second PUT of a slot is a 409 whatever the value, so a confused or hostile participant cannot replace its own commitment after the peer has read it. The same per-message byte cap, live-session cap and ten-minute TTL as the legacy relay bound the abuse surface.

404.description: An unknown role or type, or no such (or an expired) session.

409.description: The slot is already written; slots are write-once.

413.description: The message is larger than the per-message cap.

get.summary: Read one role's message from a Voidbind pairing session.
get.description: The peer polls the slot it is waiting on until it appears. Returns the opaque bytes the named role stored, or a 404 while the slot is still empty (the ordinary "keep waiting") or once the session has expired.

404.description: Not yet written, an unknown role or type, or no such session.

parameters.name: method
parameters.description: The OpenSubsonic method, optionally with the legacy `.view` suffix (`ping`, `getArtists`, `getAlbumList2`, `getAlbum`, `stream`, …). The method vocabulary is the OpenSubsonic specification's, not Heyarr's — which is why this is one compatibility endpoint rather than forty hand-written operations.

parameters.name: u
parameters.description: The Subsonic username. Carried for protocol compatibility; the credential is `p`.

parameters.name: p
parameters.description: The password a Subsonic client sends — for Heyarr, a bearer token (optionally `enc:<hex>`-encoded), mapped onto the same tokens and scopes the rest of the API uses. The salted-token pair (`t`+`s`) is NOT supported: Heyarr keeps tokens argon2id-hashed and never holds the plaintext to recompute the MD5, so it is refused with error 40.

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Response format, `xml` (default) or `json`.

parameters.name: c
parameters.description: The client application name (protocol handshake).

parameters.name: v
parameters.description: The Subsonic protocol version the client speaks.

get.summary: The OpenSubsonic compatibility adapter (§70, M11).
get.description:
A read-only projection of Heyarr's server-readable catalogue onto the OpenSubsonic REST protocol, so an existing music client can browse the library and play from it without Heyarr owning a client. It is mounted outside `/api/v1` and authenticates in the protocol's own terms, for the same reason `render` and `pair` are: a Subsonic client cannot present a Heyarr bearer credential in an `Authorization` header.

It exposes NO personal state. Playlists, play-counts, scrobbles and starred items are encrypted and opaque to the controller (Invariant 6, §72): the server holds no key, so it cannot serve them faithfully and must not fake them. They belong to a device-side Personal MCP (§73). History/starred list types return empty rather than a fabricated ranking, and the playlist methods are simply not served.

`stream` and `download` resolve a track to a blob hash and delegate to the ordinary blob route (ADR-0013): Range, 206 and progressive partial serving are inherited, and the adapter neither reimplements byte serving nor reshapes the canonical model to suit the protocol (§70).

200.description: For browse and handshake methods, the Subsonic response envelope in the requested format — always HTTP 200, with success or failure carried inside as `status`. For `stream`/`download`, the track's bytes.

206.description: A byte range of a track (`stream`/`download` with a `Range` header).

head.description: The HEAD counterpart, used by clients probing a track's size before streaming it.

get.summary: The OPDS catalog root (§69, §70, M11).
get.description:
The OPDS 1.2 compatibility adapter for publications — the Atom profile real readers speak (KOReader, Foliate, Marvin, Chunky, Panels) — as a read-only projection of Heyarr's server-readable publication catalogue, so an existing reader can browse the library and download from it without Heyarr owning a client. This is the navigation feed: a menu whose one entry descends into the acquisition feed.

Mounted outside `/api/v1` and authenticated with HTTP **Basic**, for the same reason `render`, `pair` and `rest` are outside it: an OPDS reader cannot present a Heyarr bearer credential in the group's scheme. The password a reader sends is a Heyarr bearer token, mapped onto the same tokens and `read` scope the rest of the API uses; a missing or bad credential is a real 401 with a `WWW-Authenticate: Basic` challenge.

It exposes NO personal state: reading position, bookmarks and shelves are encrypted and opaque to the controller (Invariant 6, §72) and belong to a device-side Personal MCP (§73), not this adapter.

200.description: The navigation feed, as OPDS 1.2 Atom XML.

401.description: No or bad credential; carries an HTTP Basic authentication challenge.

get.summary: The OPDS acquisition feed — every downloadable publication.
get.description: One Atom entry per book, each carrying its title and author and an acquisition link per streamable format (EPUB, PDF, CBZ, …) with that format's media type. A publication is a book Work, a format is an Edition, the bytes are an Asset; the canonical model is not reshaped to suit OPDS (§70). Only formats backed by a blob are offered — a linked asset has no bytes (ADR-0020), so it is never advertised as acquirable.

200.description: The acquisition feed, as OPDS 1.2 Atom XML.

401.description: No or bad credential; carries an HTTP Basic authentication challenge.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: The edition (format) id an acquisition link points at.

get.summary: Download one publication format.
get.description: Resolves the edition to a blob hash and a server-known media type and delegates byte serving to the ordinary blob route (ADR-0013): Range and 206 are inherited, not reimplemented, past the point where Basic auth has decided the caller may read.

401.description: No or bad credential; carries an HTTP Basic authentication challenge.

404.description: No such publication, or the edition has no downloadable blob.

head.summary: Headers for a publication download (size before fetching).
head.description: The HEAD counterpart, used by a reader probing a format's size.

get.summary: The DLNA/UPnP MediaServer device description (§70,
get.description: The root device document a UPnP control point — a television, a speaker — fetches first to learn this is a MediaServer and where its ContentDirectory service lives. Served unauthenticated, like the renderer and pairing routes, because the device that reads it has no credential to present. SSDP LAN advertisement is a tracked follow-up; a control point given this URL browses and plays without discovery.

get.summary: The ContentDirectory service description (SCPD).
get.description: Describes the one action this service implements — Browse — and the arguments it takes, so a control point can build a request. A constant document; the service does not vary per instance.

post.summary: The ContentDirectory SOAP control endpoint (Browse).
post.description: Answers the SOAP Browse action over a read-only projection of the server-readable catalogue (§70): a folder per content type, its playable items inside. The reply is DIDL-Lite whose resource URLs are render capabilities (ADR-0040) — the device fetches bytes from the unauthenticated render route, which exists precisely because it has no Authorization header. Only assets the render route can serve become items; the model is never reshaped to suit UPnP. Browse is the only action implemented; another returns a SOAP UPnPError fault, not a 404.

200.description: A BrowseResponse SOAP envelope carrying DIDL-Lite.

500.description: A SOAP fault carrying a UPnP error code (e.g. 701 no such object, 401 invalid action).

parameters.name: hash
parameters.description: The BLAKE3 digest that names the blob, as `blake3:<64 lowercase hex characters>`.

get.summary: Serve a blob's bytes, whole or by range.
get.description:
The byte-serving contract of spec §28, and deliberately one endpoint with four consumers: direct playback, remote ffprobe (§29), replication, and HTTP web-seeding (§27). See ADR-0013 — it is not "the playback endpoint" and must not be tuned as one.

The response carries a strong `ETag` derived from the content, and `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`. Immutable caching is correct here rather than risky because the URL is the digest: this path can never mean different bytes. No `Last-Modified` is sent — a modification time is a property of one peer's copy, and two peers holding identical bytes must advertise identical validators.

The media type is always `application/octet-stream`: the content store knows the digest and the length and nothing else. What the bytes mean is catalog metadata.

parameters.name: download
parameters.description: `1`, `true` or `yes` adds `Content-Disposition: attachment`. The bytes, ranges and validators are identical either way.

404.description: This peer holds no such blob. Ask another peer.

416.description: The requested range lies outside the blob.

head.summary: Report a blob's size and range support without transferring it.
head.description: Identical to `get` in every header, with no body. This is how a remote prober or a replication client learns the length and confirms range support before it starts.

200.description: The blob exists; `Content-Length` is its size.

206.description: The blob exists and the requested range is satisfiable.

416.description: The requested range lies outside the blob.

parameters.name: hash
parameters.description: The BLAKE3 digest that names the ciphertext blob, as `blake3:<64 lowercase hex characters>`.

put.summary: Upload a client-encrypted, content-addressed vault blob and pin it. Requires `write`.
put.description: The vault content ingest path (ADR-0021, ADR-0096), deliberately separate from scan-ingest and from the read-only blob GET contract. The client encrypts the bytes into fixed frames (ADR-0097) and uploads the ciphertext under the digest that names it; the server verifies the bytes hash to `{hash}`, stores them, and records a placement pin so garbage collection retains them — a vault blob has no catalog reference the control plane can see. The server never holds plaintext. Reads use `GET /blobs/{hash}/content`.

201.description: The blob was stored and pinned.

hash.description: The `blake3:<hex>` id the blob was stored under.

post.summary: Pin a vault blob to a peer OTHER than self, so it replicates there. Requires `write`.
post.description: Cross-site placement (ADR-0096). A device says a ciphertext vault blob should live on a named peer; the convergence union turns the pin into a replication target for that peer, and the pin retains the blob against garbage collection. The pin is opaque — a (blob, peer) pair with no space, path or asset link — so the control plane learns that a blob belongs on a peer, never which vault or file it is. Idempotent per (blob, peer). The peer is not checked for existence: a pin may outlive churn in `peers`, and a pin naming a peer that is not a replication target is simply ignored.

200.description: The pin, as recorded (the (blob, peer) pair it is identified by).

delete.summary: Remove a vault blob's placement pin for a peer. Requires `write`.
delete.description: Removes the pin recorded by POST (ADR-0096), so the peer is no longer a replication target for the blob and, where the pin was the blob's last reference, garbage collection may reclaim it. A pin is identified by its (blob, peer) pair, so the body carries the same two fields as POST. Idempotent: removing a pin that is not there is a 204, not a 404.

204.description: The pin is gone (or was already).

get.summary: Page the peers.
get.description:
A paginated collection even though Milestone 1 has exactly one peer
(ADR-0010). A client written against a single-object response would have
to be rewritten for Milestone 4, and the ones that are not keep showing
one peer.

post.summary: Enrol a peer, or move an existing member's endpoint.
post.description:
Peer enrolment is operator-mediated and explicit (§26, ADR-0012). There
is no discovery, no join token and no trust on first use: an operator
reads the other node's public key out of `GET /api/v1/peers` at that
site and posts it here, and the operator at the other site does the
same in the other direction.

The public key decides what this does. A key nobody holds is an
enrolment and answers `201` with a `Location`. A key this instance
already pins is the same peer, and the request may move its `endpoint`,
`site` or `mode` — that answers `200`, because nothing was created and
a client treating `201` as "a peer joined" would count it twice. A key
already pinned to a peer with a DIFFERENT name is refused: a peer is
its key, not its name.

Admin, not write, and for a stronger reason than the token endpoints:
membership is the only trust root in the inter-peer path, so a
credential that could enrol a peer could hand a complete replica of the
library to a machine of its choosing.

200.description:
The key was already a member. Its endpoint, site or mode may have
moved; its identity did not.

400.description:
The public key is missing, or malformed — the wrong algorithm
prefix, not lowercase hex, or not 32 bytes. Or the `endpoint` was
given and cannot be dialled: a scheme other than `https` or
`unix`, no host, a port that is not a number, or a path where an
origin belongs.

The endpoint is refused HERE rather than by whatever first tries to
use it, because registration is idempotent on the key: a typo
replaces a working endpoint, and the peer stays enrolled and looks
healthy while being unreachable.

409.description:
The key is registered to another peer, the name is taken by a peer
with a different key, or the registration claimed to be this node
and this node already exists.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description:
The peer's id or its name. Both, because an operator holds whichever
of the two they were shown, and a lookup that accepted only the id
would send them to the list first — which is the step that gets
skipped when the thing being looked up is about to be removed.

get.summary: Show one peer.

delete.description:
ADR-0012: "Revocation is removing a membership record." There is no
revocation list and no certificate to expire — the record IS the trust,
so deleting it withdraws the trust.

Membership is consulted on every request rather than at process start,
so a removed peer stops being able to read bytes immediately, on the
connection it is already holding open. The peer's `replicas` rows go
with it: a peer this instance will not talk to is not a peer whose copy
counts towards placement.

It answers with the record it removed rather than `204`, so that "did I
revoke the right peer?" is not a question answered by re-reading the
list you just changed. This node cannot remove itself.

200.description: The membership record that was revoked.

409.description: The peer is this node, which cannot revoke itself.

post.summary: Ask for this peer's convergence to be re-examined.
post.description:
§19, §57. **Enqueues** a `reconcile_peer` job; it does not run one.
Reconciliation is a job (invariant 4, ADR-0002) and the worker that
runs it may be another process, so this answers `202` rather than
pretending to be the worker.

The job diffs §19's desired blob set — for a Full Peer, the complete
canonical Blob set — against what this peer's inventory reports, and
enqueues `replicate_blob` for the difference. It emits the work and
stops there; moving the bytes is a separate job.

Deduped per peer, so asking repeatedly while a cycle is queued yields
one job. Convergence also runs fabric-wide on a beat, so this is for
impatience — a peer just enrolled, or just restored — rather than for
correctness.

`write` rather than `admin`, unlike enrolment and revocation: it
changes nothing about who is trusted.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: The peer's id or its name, as for `GET /api/v1/peers/{id}`.

post.summary: Force two-site catalog convergence now (§49, ADR-0073).
post.description:
Runs one pass of the editorial catalog op-log exchange with every
sibling, immediately, rather than waiting for the beat: this node offers
its ops to each sibling over the pinned peer link and records the merged
G-set each answers with, so a delete made here reaches the other site
now (ADR-0073, #449).

Unlike `/api/v1/peers/{id}/reconcile`, this RUNS the exchange rather than
enqueueing a job — the exchange is a bounded RPC, not bulk byte movement
— so it answers `200` with what converged, not `202`. Idempotent: the
op-log is a G-set, and an unreachable sibling is deferred, not an error.

`write`, not `admin`: it propagates ops already recorded, changing
nothing about who is trusted. A single-site node with no sibling answers
`503`.

200.description: The pass ran; how many siblings converged and how many deferred.

503.description: This node converges a catalog with no sibling.

get.summary: Page the replicas.
What ffprobe said about a blob's bytes.
get.description:
Hangs off the blob rather than the asset because a probe describes
**bytes**, and bytes are identity: two assets sharing a blob share one
probe (§29, invariant 1).

A blob with no probe is **404, not an empty 200**. "We have not probed
this" and "this has no streams" are different answers, and a client
that cannot tell them apart cannot decide whether to wait — which is
exactly the state every blob is in on a node with no ffprobe
(ADR-0023).

`bytes_read` and `materialised` are how the probe was obtained, exposed
so §29 is auditable in a running deployment. An instance where every
probe materialised is one where remote probing is silently not working,
and the only other symptom is that it feels slow.

get.summary: Page publications — EPUB, PDF, CBZ and CBR.
get.description:
Heyarr **stores and serves** publications; it does not render them
(§69). Clients render.

This is the catalog view: enough to tell an EPUB from a CBZ, and how
long it is, without downloading it first. The bytes come from
`/api/v1/blobs/{hash}/content` like everything else — ADR-0013 makes
that one endpoint with several consumers, and a reader is another one,
not another endpoint.

get.summary: One publication, by ASSET id.
get.description:
Keyed by asset rather than blob. The metadata is stored against the
blob because it describes the bytes, but a client holds an asset: one
blob can be two assets with two filenames in two libraries, and "which
publication" is a question about a *use* of the bytes.

post.summary: Plan, open a session, and return somewhere to play from.
post.description:
The one call a client makes when someone presses play.

**The controller stays out of the content data path (§32).** It returns
a direct URL to the peer holding the replica; it does not proxy bytes.
A controller that proxied would make playback's availability depend on
its own, which is exactly the coupling §53's degraded-operation model
exists to avoid — a Full Peer must keep streaming when the controller
has gone.

The URL is `/api/v1/blobs/{hash}/content`, unchanged. ADR-0013's
consequences forbid "adding a player-shaped session token" to it, so
playback gets no byte route, no auth scheme and no signed URL of its
own — it gets a short-lived credential and the same endpoint
replication and the BitTorrent web-seed use.

**The credential is scoped to `read` and expires, but is not scoped to
one blob.** A client holding one can read any blob until it expires.
Per-blob scoping is a *grant* (§77's `/grants`), which is a later
milestone with principals behind it; inventing a lesser version here
would be a second authorisation model to reconcile with the real one.

**Anything that is not DIRECT is a 409** carrying the planner's first
reason, not a 501. The request is well-formed and the asset is real;
what cannot happen is this pairing of asset and device. No session is
opened — a session for a playback that cannot happen is state nobody
will clean up, and it would appear in "continue watching" for something
nobody watched. `POST /playback/plan` has the full rationale.

201.description: The session, the plan, and where to play from.

409.description:
The plan is not DIRECT, or nothing holds the bytes. No session was
opened.

post.summary: Queue a remux for an asset a device cannot take as it is (§10, §75).
post.description:
Rewraps the encoded streams into a container the device declares. It
does **not** re-encode: `-c copy` is the whole contract, and Milestone
2 has no quality ladder, no HLS or DASH segmenting and no transcode.

**Separate from `POST /playback` deliberately.** A remux is minutes of
work and disk; starting one because a client asked what it could play
would let a browsing client fill a disk. When to spend that is a policy
question, and policy is §55's.

Only a **REMUX** plan is actionable. A DIRECT plan needs no work, and a
TRANSCODE plan would produce a remux that still does not play — a
failure the client would discover only after waiting for it. Both are
409.

Returns the job. Poll `/jobs/{id}` or follow `job.*` on the event
stream, then re-plan.

The output is recorded as an **Asset** with role `derived` on the same
Edition, so replication, integrity and garbage collection treat it like
any other managed asset. That means it will be replicated and will be
reclaimed when nothing references it — both correct, neither free.

409.description: The plan is not REMUX, so there is nothing useful to queue.

post.summary: Extract embedded subtitles from already-ingested video (ADR-0084).
post.description:
Queues an `extract_subtitles` job for every managed video in scope whose
Edition has no subtitle yet.

Extraction otherwise runs at ingest, so a video ingested before ADR-0084
— or before this node had ffmpeg — has embedded tracks that were never
lifted out, and a rescan does not fix it: the bytes are unchanged, the
ingest deduplicates, and nothing re-enqueues. This is the operator's
lever to reprocess that existing content once.

A scope is required — `library_id`, `work_id`, or `all` — so "this one
show" is never one forgotten flag from "every video on the node". Only
videos with no subtitle are touched, and the extract job is a no-op on a
video with no embedded text tracks, so a re-run is cheap and safe.

post.summary: Request subtitles for held content that has none (ADR-0085).
post.description:
Creates a subtitle want for every managed video in scope that holds no
subtitle in the requested language. The fetch driver then acquires each
from a subtitle provider.

This is the door for a subtitle that exists NOWHERE — neither shipped
beside the video nor embedded in its container (`/subtitles/backfill`
covers those). A `language` is required — a subtitle want is for a
language and there is no default to fetch — and a scope is required
(`library_id`, `work_id`, or `all`) so "this one show" is never one
forgotten flag from "every video on the node".

Idempotent: a video that already holds a subtitle of the language is
skipped, and a want that already exists is left alone, so a re-run only
creates the genuinely-missing.

post.summary: Enrich held music/book works now (ADR-0087).
post.description:
Queues an `enrich_work` job for every held music/book work in scope that
still lacks a cover or a canonical id, ignoring the enrich beat's backoff
schedule.

Enrichment otherwise runs on a background beat. This is the operator's
lever to enrich a scope now — after wiring an enrich provider, or after
ingesting a shelf of books. A scope is required — `library_id`, `work_id`,
`author`, or `all` — so "this one author" is never one forgotten flag
from "every book on the node". Only under-enriched works are touched and
the enrich job is idempotent, so a re-run is cheap and safe. Refused with
400 when the node has no enrich provider configured (the jobs would never
run).

get.summary: How many held music/book works still need enrichment (ADR-0087).
get.description:
Reports the enrich backlog: how many held music/book works still lack a
cover or a canonical id, out of the total held, so a person can watch a
backfill drain.

post.summary: What should this device do with this asset? (§68)
post.description:
DIRECT, REMUX, TRANSCODE — or `unplayable` when nothing holds the bytes.

**It writes nothing and opens no session.** A client shows a "play"
button by planning and opens a session when someone presses it; if
planning created state, every hover would too.

The `reasons` are the point. "Why is my television transcoding this" is
the single most common question this class of software is asked, and a
planner that answers only with a verb cannot answer it. Codes are
stable strings because clients branch on them; `detail` is prose for a
human and may change.

**Media nothing has probed plans DIRECT**, with a `no_probe` reason
saying the plan is a guess. The conservative-looking answer is
TRANSCODE and it is wrong: a node with no probes is precisely a node
with no ffprobe (ADR-0023), which cannot transcode either — so
planning TRANSCODE there would make the entire library unplayable,
while DIRECT makes most of it work and fails visibly when it does not.

**A client that says what it can decode gets the leg (ADR-0069).**
Send `client` — the containers, video and audio codecs it decodes and
a height ceiling — instead of, or as well as, `device_id`, and the
answer additionally carries `mode`, `url`, `mime`, `reason` and
`source`:

- `mode: direct` — fetch `url`, which is the ordinary blob endpoint.
- `mode: stream` — fetch `url`, which is
  `GET /api/v1/playback/stream/{token}`: an on-the-fly fragmented MP4
  with the video copied where the client decodes it and the audio
  re-encoded to stereo AAC where it does not (the AC-3 and MP2
  cases), the whole thing re-wrapped when the container is the
  problem (AVI), and the video re-encoded and capped to `max_height`
  only when the client cannot decode the picture. `reason` says which.
- `mode: unplayable` — no peer holds the bytes; `reason` is routing's.

With `client`, media nothing has probed is **probed now** when this
node has ffprobe and holds the bytes, and the result is cached in
`blob_probes` exactly as a worker's probe would be. A stream is
produced only by the node holding the replica; a controller routing
to another peer answers `direct` on that peer and says why. A node
with no ffmpeg answers `direct` with the reason and the note that it
cannot repackage — the bytes and the truth, not a black player.

get.summary: The on-the-fly repackage a `stream` plan points at (ADR-0069).
get.description:
Fragmented MP4 (`video/mp4`), produced by one ffmpeg per request from
the blob the token names, written as it is made. The token is what
`POST /playback/plan` returned in `url` for `mode: stream`: signed by
this node, bound to the blob, to the repackage the planner decided
(copy or re-encode, per stream, and the height cap), and to the
**credential that asked for the plan** — present it with any other
credential and it is refused. It is good for an hour from planning;
the stream itself is not cut off at expiry, only its start is.

**No ranges, no `Content-Length`, no seeking in v1.** The bytes do not
exist until ffmpeg produces them, so a `Range` header is ignored and
the response is a `200` with no length. A player treats this as a
live, unseekable stream — Media3 does, given fragmented MP4 with no
Range support. To seek, re-request with `?start=<seconds>`: a new
request restarts ffmpeg with an input seek from that instant.

The node runs at most `media.stream_concurrency` of these at once
(default two — each is an ffmpeg, and one re-encoding video is a
core). Past the cap the answer is `429` with `Retry-After`, never a
queue: a client waiting on a stream that has not started is a black
player. When the client disconnects, ffmpeg is killed at once.

Every refusal of the token — bad signature, expired, another
credential's, a blob this node does not hold — is the same opaque
`404`; the reason goes to the log under a bounded label.

Same authentication as everything else under `/api/v1`: `read` scope,
Bearer or Device.

parameters.name: start
parameters.description: Restart the stream from this many seconds into the source.

Cache-Control.description: `no-store` — the bytes are produced per request.

404.description:
The token does not verify, has expired, was planned for another
credential, or names bytes this node does not hold. Deliberately
one answer for all four.

429.description: Every stream slot on this node is in use. `Retry-After` is set.

get.summary: Page consumption sessions, newest first.
get.description:
`?state=resumable` is the **"continue watching"** query: every session
that has not reached a terminal state, most recently touched first, for
watching, listening and reading alike (§67).

It is a named filter rather than `state=created,playing,paused` because
"resumable" is the question clients actually ask, and spelling it as
three states would put the state machine's shape into every client.

post.summary: Open a consumption session.
post.description:
One model covers watching, listening and reading (§67, ADR-0024). The
session starts in `created` — a real state, not a formality: the gap
between "I intend to watch this" and "bytes are moving" is where the
planner runs, and collapsing it makes an abandoned plan
indistinguishable from a playback that stalled instantly.

get.summary: One session.

post.summary: Move a session through its state machine.
post.description:
One endpoint rather than six (`/start`, `/pause`, `/resume`, …),
because the state machine is one thing: six endpoints would each need
to know the transition table, and the first one to disagree with it
would be a session in a state the domain says is impossible.

Every transition emits a `playback.session.*` event, inside the same
transaction that wrote the row (invariant 7, ADR-0009).

An illegal transition — resuming a completed session, progressing a
stopped one — is **409**, not 400. The request is well-formed and would
be legal against a different state, and a client cannot tell "you sent
nonsense" from "you are out of date" if both are 400. Only the second
is fixed by re-reading the session.

409.description: The transition is illegal from the session's current state.

get.summary: Page the registered devices.
get.description: Ordered by `(name, id)`.

post.summary: Register a device, or update the one already registered.
post.description:
An **upsert on `device_key`**, not a create. An app announces itself on
every launch; if that created a row each time, this collection would
fill with duplicates named "Living Room" and the playback planner would
be choosing between four thousand copies of one television.

`201` with a `Location` header the first time, `200` afterwards.

A device here is a **capability profile, not an identity** (§68).
Nothing in it is a credential and nothing is authenticated: Heyarr has
no way to interrogate a television, so a client declares what it can
play and Heyarr believes it. Device enrolment, keypairs and key
recovery are ADR-0022 and Milestone 8.

Codec and container names are lower-cased, trimmed and de-duplicated,
so two clients spelling one capability differently converge rather than
producing a planner that matches one device and not its identical twin.

200.description: The device already existed; its profile was updated.

get.summary: One device.
Page what should exist.
get.description:
Ordered by `(created_at, id)`. A want has no name to sort by, and the
interesting order is the order things were asked for.

parameters.name: monitor
parameters.description: Only monitored, or only unmonitored, wants.

parameters.name: upgradable
parameters.description:
Which wants are in a state where an upgrade **could** happen — the
listing question §71's `get_upgrade_candidates` asks.

Answered from **state alone**: monitored, content satisfied, and
holding bytes. It deliberately does not score anything, because
whether a want has reached its profile's *terminal* condition needs
the incumbent re-evaluated against the profile — a join and a
scorer per row, which would run the evaluator hundreds of times to
render one page.

So this filter is the **cheap half** of eligibility and is a
superset: a want that is monitored and satisfied but already
terminal appears here. `GET /desired/{id}/satisfaction` reports the
terminal test per want, and the `upgrade_scan` job applies it.

post.summary: Want something.
post.description:
**A want must work when you have nothing.** That is the whole point of
this endpoint and the requirement most easily lost: every fixture in
this repository has assets, so a design that only works once something
exists passes every test and fails the first real use.

Name the work either by `work_id`, or — when it does not exist yet — by
a `work` descriptor of content type, title and year. The descriptor
resolves through the **same** `(content_type, work_key)` get-or-create
the scanner uses, so wanting a film and later scanning it converge on
one Work rather than producing two.

Name the quality profile by `quality_profile_id` or by
`quality_profile` (its name) — a person writing this by hand knows
`living-room`, not a UUID. A profile is **required**: "this should
exist", with no statement of what would count as existing, cannot be
evaluated (§56).

`monitor` defaults to **true**. Wanting something and then silently
never looking for anything better is the surprising default.

Two wants over the same target with **different** profiles are legal
and are the point (§61 — never one version per title): the living-room
copy and the phone-sized copy are two wants. The same target with the
same profile is one want written twice, and is a `409`.

409.description: That content is already wanted under that profile.

get.summary: One desired item.

patch.summary: Change the conditions, the monitoring or the note.
patch.description:
An omitted field is left alone.

**The target cannot be changed.** Repointing a want at different
content is not an edit, it is a different want, and allowing it would
make the acquisition history attached to this row describe something
else. Delete it and want the other thing.

A request that changes nothing emits no event.

200.description: The want as it now stands.

409.description: The new profile would duplicate an existing want.

delete.description:
Physical, matching quality profiles and for the same reason: a want is
a statement of intent, not bytes. ADR-0018's logical-delete stance
exists to stop shared, expensive, unrecoverable bytes being unlinked
inline, and none of that applies here — an operator who says they no
longer want something should find it gone.

The `desired.removed` event carries the target, not only the row id, so
the log still says what was wanted after the row is gone.

get.summary: What the last search found, and why each release was judged so.
get.description:
§63 says evaluation is deterministic and **inspectable**. This is the
inspectable half: an evaluation that lived in memory for two hundred
milliseconds is deterministic and cannot answer "why did it pick that
release, last Tuesday, at 3am".

The **rejections matter more than the acceptance**. A search that found
twelve releases and took none of them leaves twelve explained refusals
here, because a want that simply goes quiet is the failure mode §60
keeps explainable rejection reasons to avoid.

It reads what the last search **stored**, and deliberately does not
re-search or re-score. Re-running the scorer would answer a different
question — what would be decided *now* — and that substitution is
exactly what makes an audit trail worthless.

Ordered best first, by the same total order the scorer ranks by:
accepted above rejected, then score descending, then the provider's
candidate id. The listing and the selection therefore cannot disagree
about which is best.

post.summary: Look for releases that would satisfy this want, now.
post.description:
§60's **manual search** — the same job the schedule runs, triggered by
a person, with the results visible whether or not anything was
acceptable.

**Enqueues** a job; it does not run one. A search is a job (invariant
4, ADR-0002) and the worker that runs it may be another process, so
this answers `202` rather than pretending to be the worker — and rather
than holding a request open across a provider round trip an indexer may
take thirty seconds to refuse.

Deduped per want, so asking repeatedly while one is queued yields one
job. Per want rather than globally: two wants should be searched
concurrently, and collapsing them would make a library of two hundred
wants take two hundred sequential searches to make one pass.

On a node with **no indexer** the job stays *pending and visible*
rather than failing (ADR-0025) — it is work waiting for a capability,
not work that went wrong.

post.summary: Re-drive the import for a want whose ingest wedged.
post.description:
Re-run the hash-and-import for a want stuck in `verifying` or
`ingesting` — a download that finished but whose ingest job was lost (a
worker crash mid-lease, a node OOM, a client that dropped the completed
transfer before it ran), leaving the want with no job driving it.

**Enqueues** the same `ingest_acquisition` job the download poll would;
the ingest worker re-locates and re-verifies the bytes itself, so no
download-client state is needed. **Idempotent** — the dedupe key means
an ingest already running is left alone, so this answers `202` and
reaches only wants with no live ingest.

The stuck-ingest watchdog does this automatically once a want has been
wedged past a grace window; this is the same action on demand.

post.summary: Take this release, whatever the ranking says.
post.description:
§60's **manual override**, and it is a different feature from manual
search: a search asks what is out there, an override says which one to
take.

It **records that it was an override**, and what the scorer had chosen
instead. An override that left no trace would look exactly like an
ordinary selection, and "why did it take that one" would then have no
answer — which is the property §60's deterministic scoring exists to
give.

### It refuses a candidate the profile rejected

A `409`, deliberately. The gates in §62 are the operator's own
statement of what is acceptable, and an override that could ignore them
would quietly turn `accept` into a suggestion. Wanting something
outside the profile is perfectly expressible — by **changing the
profile**, which is visible and durable, rather than by a one-off that
leaves the profile saying something nobody means.

Naming the candidate the scorer already chose is a selection rather
than an override, and is not recorded as a disagreement: putting a
departure in the audit trail that never happened is its own kind of
wrong.

candidate_id.description:
The **provider's** id for the release, as returned by
`/candidates`.

404.description:
No candidate with that id for this want — it may have been
superseded by a later search.

409.description: That candidate was rejected by the quality profile.

post.summary: Adopt bytes that have already arrived (§65).
post.description:
"These bytes are here, they answer this want, take them."

§65 lists many ways bytes arrive, and a polled download client is only
the ordinary one. A client Heyarr does **not** poll is an ordinary
situation too: a transfer that finished before Heyarr knew about it,
something fetched by hand, or a client the registry has no integration
for.

The pipeline afterwards is **identical** to the polled path — the same
verification, the same ingest job, the same §64 edges. The only thing
that differs is who noticed the transfer had finished.

`local_path` is where the bytes are **in a namespace Heyarr can open**,
not the download client's. Path mapping is the poller's job and there
is no client here to map from.

This is deliberately **not an upload**: Heyarr is told where the bytes
already are rather than receiving them. An upload is a different §65
source with a different shape, and conflating them would put a
multi-gigabyte body on an endpoint whose whole job is a path.

Answers `202`: the hash and the ingest are a job, because hashing a
large file is real work and the worker that does it may be another
process (invariant 4).

Adopting the same transfer twice is harmless — the acquisition is keyed
on `(provider, external_id)` and the ingest job is deduped per want.

provider.description:
What produced the bytes. Free text: this endpoint exists
precisely for clients the registry does not know about.

external_id.description:
That producer's identifier — an infohash, a job id. It is
what makes adopting the same transfer twice idempotent
rather than duplicative.

local_path.description: Where the bytes are, in Heyarr's own namespace.

409.description: That want already has an acquisition in flight.

get.summary: Why a want is, or is not, satisfied.
get.description:
The acquisition state on a `DesiredItem` says **what** the answer is.
This says **why** — and it is what makes "I have this film, why does
Heyarr say it is missing" answerable, which is the question this axis
gets asked most often.

It **reconciles** rather than reading a cached answer, for the same
reason the evaluation endpoint scores rather than replays: an
explanation that might be minutes stale is one nobody can trust while
they are looking at a file they can see on disk.

Per want rather than inlined on the listing, because a page of fifty
wants would carry fifty evaluations of several rules each.

### The two axes are evaluated separately (§56)

Content asks "do we hold bytes the quality profile accepts?" — and
**existing is not satisfying**: a 480p rip under a 1080p-minimum
profile is content *present* and content *not satisfied*. Conflating
them makes the upgrade workflow unreachable.

Placement asks "are those bytes on every Full Peer that should hold
them?", and it is asked only of **the bytes that satisfy** — asking it
of a rejected copy would report a want as fully satisfied because the
wrong file is well replicated.

post.summary: Ask for this want to be re-examined.
post.description:
**Enqueues** a job; it does not run one. Reconciliation is a job
(invariant 4, ADR-0002) and the worker that runs it may be another
process, so this answers `202` rather than pretending to be the worker.

Deduped per want, so asking repeatedly while one is queued yields one
job. Reconciliation also runs on a beat and when a want is created, so
this is for impatience rather than for correctness.

get.summary: List every followed source.
get.description:
A followed source is a standing subscription that archives everything a
source emits (§55, M12). Each entry carries the derived counts a person
actually wants — how many items its feed has yielded, and how many are
archived — plus when it was last polled, when it is due next, and whether
its feed adapter is healthy.

post.summary: Follow a source.
post.description:
Subscribe to a source and archive everything it emits, forever — a
**standing subscription**, distinct from `POST /desired` (`want_content`),
which gets one thing once.

**Source-agnostic (#396).** There is no `source`, `provider` or
`feed_type` field. Give a content intent (which series) and an identity
(a `url`, or an explicit `tvdb_id`); the system **infers** the type. Phase
1 implements `tv_series` only — anything else is refused with a message
