that says so, rather than being stored and never polled.

The series work is resolved exactly as `want_content` resolves a work: an
existing `work_id`, or a `title` (and optional `year`) that
get-or-creates the series work, so a follow and a later scan converge on
one work.

201.description: The source is now followed; its first poll has been queued.

get.summary: One followed source.
get.description:
A detail screen otherwise re-reads the whole list and picks its id out
of it (#430).

delete.description:
Stops future polls. `keep_archive` defaults to `true` — it keeps every
item and asset already archived. Removing the archive (`keep_archive=false`)
is not implemented in Phase 1 and is refused rather than silently ignored.

parameters.name: keep_archive
parameters.description: Keep what was already archived. Defaults to true; false is refused in Phase 1.

patch.summary: Repoint a followed source at a different quality profile.
patch.description:
Change which quality profile a subscription — and every want it has
already projected — is judged against, in place, without unfollowing it
(ADR-0082). The held wants are re-judged against the new profile at once,
so an article feed moved from a video profile to `published` has its
captured articles counted as archived immediately.

Change the profile, the backfill, or both; a field left out is left as
it is, and a body that changes nothing is refused (a repoint is an
explicit act, not a reset to a default). Name the profile with exactly
one of `quality_profile_id` or `quality_profile`. Moving `backfill` to
`full` queues a poll at once, so the back-catalogue a `from_now` follow
skipped is projected without waiting for the next scheduled round.

quality_profile_id.description: The profile to move to, by id. Give this or quality_profile, not both.

quality_profile.description: The profile to move to, by name (e.g. "published"). Give this or quality_profile_id, not both.

backfill.description: How much back-catalogue polls project from now on. `full` queues a poll immediately.

want_subtitles.description:
Replace the subtitle languages (ISO-639-1) this source projects a
subtitle want for (ADR-0085). Omit to leave them unchanged; an empty
array wants none. Like backfill, felt on the next poll (queued now).

200.description: The repointed subscription, with items_archived reflecting the re-judged wants.

get.summary: What this source has archived, and what it merely knows about.
get.description:
The Items the source's feed has yielded (ADR-0056), each with the
item-scoped want the source projected for it and that want's
acquisition axes (ADR-0057/0059) — the archive a person reads to answer
"what has this subscription actually got me" (#430).

`want` is **null** for an item no want was projected for: a
`backfill=from_now` source knows about back-catalogue episodes it
deliberately did not ask for, and reporting them rather than omitting
them is what makes this an archive and not a queue.

Paged by `item_key`, the source-stable identity the feed is stable on,
so a re-poll that inserts an older episode cannot shuffle the pages
under a reader.

200.description: A page of the source's items.

post.summary: Poll every followed source now.
post.description:
Force every followed source to poll now rather than waiting for each
one's scheduled `next_poll_at` (ADR-0078) — the bulk sibling of
`POST /followed-sources/{id}/poll`, useful for refreshing many feeds at
once or after a controller was down.

**Enqueues** the follow beat's own `poll_source` job per source (§55,
invariant 4/ADR-0002); it does not poll inline. Best-effort per source:
one source failing to enqueue is skipped rather than failing the sweep.
Deduped per source, so a source already carrying a queued poll is not
polled twice, and no source's schedule is advanced — these are **extra**
polls, not reschedules. An empty library is a valid, empty sweep.

202.description: A poll was queued for each source; the ids queued are returned.

post.summary: Poll this followed source now.
post.description:
Force one followed source to poll now rather than waiting for its
scheduled `next_poll_at`, which the `feed-poll` cadence puts up to six
hours out (§55, ADR-0078). Reach for it right after following something,
or when a feed is known to have just posted.

**Enqueues** the follow beat's own `poll_source` job — the same job the
follow door queues at follow time and the beat queues on the tick — and
answers `202` rather than pretending to be the worker (invariant 4,
ADR-0002). Deduped per source, so asking again while a poll is still
queued returns the same live job rather than a second one; harmless to
call repeatedly.

This is an **extra** poll, not a reschedule: the source's `next_poll_at`
is left exactly as it was (ADR-0078). On a node with **no feed adapter**
the job stays *pending and visible* rather than failing (ADR-0025).

post.summary: Find a work by what it is.
post.description:
A content-intent search over the library's works, by title and/or content
type (§55, #396). **No source parameter**: the question is what a work IS,
not which service to ask. It matches the normalised `sort_title` a scan
records, so "the conversation" finds "The Conversation".

A `POST` under the read floor, because the intent travels in a body — the
same reasoning as `POST /quality-profiles/{id}/evaluate`.

200.description:
The works that matched, each with its attributes and poster, and the
parts of a work that matched by their own title (ADR-0075): a
scanned episode with its file, or an item a followed source
projected. Both lists are always present, `[]` when empty. A
`content_type`-only search lists works and looks for no episodes.

get.summary: The continue rail — the newest unfinished session per work.
get.description:
"Continue watching / listening / reading" as a client draws it
(ADR-0075): for every work with a session that holds a position and is
not finished (`playing`, `paused` or `stopped` with a recorded locator),
the NEWEST such session, with the work and its poster, the edition
(season/episode for a series) and the asset with its probed duration
inlined — everything a card and a resume need in one read.

Distinct from `GET /consumption/sessions?state=resumable`, which is the
state machine's non-terminal set (`created`, `playing`, `paused`) and
lists every session: a rail includes a `stopped` session someone walked
away from, excludes a `created` one that never recorded anything, and
shows one card per work.

History is per-identity (ADR-0024), so a Guest is refused (ADR-0074).

parameters.name: device_id
parameters.description: Only sessions on this device.

post.summary: Find content the library does not already hold.
post.description:
A live metadata-provider search for candidate works, INCLUDING ones the
library has never seen (§55, #451) — the "not-yet-in-library" door beside
`POST /search`. Where `/search` is an offline `LIKE` over the library's
`works`, this asks the configured metadata provider (TVDB, ADR-0050/0058)
for series matching a free-text title, and returns each with the
`tvdb_id` a client passes straight to `POST /followed-sources` to bring it
in — "search then follow" in one step.

A `POST` under the read floor, because the intent travels in a body and it
writes nothing — a discovery search enters nothing into the library, it
only reports what a follow WOULD name.

`503` when this node has no metadata provider that can look content up:
the request was well-formed and nothing failed, there is simply nothing
configured to answer — distinct from a `400` (bad request) and a `500`
(server failure).

200.description: The candidate works that matched, deduplicated across providers.

503.description: No metadata provider is configured that can search for new content.

get.summary: The calling credential's own authority.
get.description:
A caller's own identity and effective authority (ADR-0061, M12) — the one
endpoint a browser/TV client reads to decide whether to show management UI
and, when it may not yet, which device key an operator must authorise.

A web-login session (ADR-0053) is read-only by default, so `POST`/`DELETE
/followed-sources` 403 from it. The interim path to write is a
**follow-management grant**: an operator authorises the session's approving
`device_key`, and the session then carries `write`. A client drives it as:
read `/session` → if `can_write` is false, show `device_key` and prompt the
operator → operator issues `POST /session/management-grants` → read
`/session` again, now `can_write`. Device-cert enrolment (ADR-0048) is the
eventual convergence that binds authority to the surface itself.

A read under the router's read floor; every authenticated caller may read
its own identity.

get.summary: The devices authorised to manage followed sources.
get.description:
Every follow-management grant (ADR-0061) — the approving device keys an
operator has authorised to hold `write` in their web-login sessions.
Listing a credential operation's state is an **admin** action, like listing
tokens.

200.description: The authorised devices, newest grant first.

post.summary: Authorise a device to manage followed sources.
post.description:
The operator's explicit consent step (ADR-0061): authorise a specific
approving `device_key` so every web-login session that device approves
carries `write`. This is the interim, non-gated path a trusted personal
device takes to manage followed sources before device-cert enrolment
(ADR-0048) converges the surface.

Idempotent: re-granting an already authorised device updates its note
rather than failing. Issuing a grant elevates a device's authority, so it
is an **admin** action, like minting a token.

The default — no grant — is read-only, so a shared surface (a TV) stays
read-only until its approver is explicitly authorised. The sharp edge is
honest and recorded in ADR-0061: the grant follows the approving device,
not the surface.

delete.description:
Remove a device's `write` authorization (ADR-0061). Its web-login sessions
return to the read floor on their next request — the grant lookup is per
request, so revocation is not deferred to a token expiry. An **admin**
action; a revoke of a device that was never granted is a 404, not a silent
success.

parameters.name: device_key
parameters.description: The approving device key to revoke ("ed25519:<hex>").

get.summary: What external services are configured, and whether they work.
get.description:
§59 centralises provider configuration. Content types do not maintain
separate registries — a new provider kind is a new **capability** here,
never a second registry (§61, §83).

### Why this endpoint exists

A node with no indexer and no download client is a **supported, tested
configuration** (ADR-0025): it scans, ingests, catalogues, verifies,
serves ranges and plays, and search and acquire jobs sit *pending and
visible* rather than failing. The cost of that design is that "why is
nothing being acquired?" has an entirely legitimate answer which is
invisible unless something reports it. This is that report.

### No credential is ever returned

Not the API key, not an endpoint with credentials embedded in it, not a
length-preserving hint. What an operator needs is which provider, what
it can do, and whether it works.

### Health is observed, not asserted

`healthy` is what the last check **found**, by exercising the provider
— a provider that reported itself healthy because it was configured
would be advertising something it might not deliver, and work would
route to it and then fail.

An **absent `checked_at` means never checked**, which is deliberately
distinct from `healthy: false`: "nobody has looked" and "we looked and
it is broken" lead to different actions. The same distinction §56's
satisfaction axes make.

Health is read from the database rather than from the answering
process's memory, because under ADR-0002 the worker that ran the check
may be another machine.

200.description: Every configured provider, and what this node can therefore do.

get.summary: Which nodes in the fleet can do what, proven by execution.
get.description:
The fleet-wide capability view (§6, §75, ADR-0040).

### Why this is not `/api/v1/system`

`/api/v1/system` describes **the node answering the request**. The
toolchain that decides whether a transcode runs is the one on the
*worker* that claims the job, and in a split-process deployment
(ADR-0002) that is another machine. ADR-0023 named this gap in its own
consequences and deferred it; this closes it.

### A capability here was PROVEN, never parsed

`ffmpeg -encoders` will happily **list** a hardware AV1 encoder on
silicon that cannot encode AV1, then fail at runtime with `No capable
devices found` — while the same device decodes AV1 fine. Encode and
decode support are asymmetric per hardware generation and the asymmetry
is not derivable from anything FFmpeg prints.

So a `probe` capability means a worker really encoded a handful of
frames from a synthetic source to a null sink with that encoder, and the
process exited successfully. Nothing else produces one.

### Advertisements NARROW, and they expire

A capability that stops passing stops being advertised — without the
binary changing and without a restart, because a device can be claimed
by another process or broken by a kernel update. An advertisement that
could only grow would lie after the first driver update.

Every advertisement carries an `expires_at` and is filtered out once it
passes: a worker that dies cannot tidy up after itself, and a power cut
is exactly the death that skips a shutdown hook.

### `?capability=` is an EXACT match

`ffmpeg` is a prefix of `ffmpeg.encoder.hevc`. A prefix match would
answer "which nodes can encode AV1" with every node that merely has
FFmpeg installed, which is the failure this whole mechanism exists to
prevent.

parameters.name: capability
parameters.description:
Return only workers holding exactly this capability string. The
vocabulary is dotted and hierarchical — `ffmpeg`,
`ffmpeg.encoder.hevc`, `ffmpeg.encoder.av1.vaapi` — and the match is
equality on the whole string, never a prefix.

200.description: Every live advertisement, and the union across the fleet.

post.summary: MCP, as JSON-RPC 2.0 over a single endpoint.
post.description:
Model Context Protocol (§71, ADR-0019). One route, because MCP
multiplexes over JSON-RPC methods rather than over paths.

Mounted here rather than on a server of its own so it inherits this
API's middleware chain, request correlation and `read` scope floor. The
**per-tool scope check** turns that floor into a contract: an MCP
session is not a new trust domain, and a `read` token calling
`want_content` is refused with JSON-RPC code `-32001`.

### Methods

| method | does |
|---|---|
| `initialize` | handshake; returns protocol version, server info and instructions |
| `tools/list` | the tool surface, each with its hand-written input schema and required scope |
| `tools/call` | invoke one tool |
| `ping` | keepalive |

A request with no `id` is a notification and is answered with `202` and
an empty body, per JSON-RPC — some clients treat a reply to one as a
protocol violation.

### What is deliberately absent

MCP's value is **semantic actions over desired state, not a second read
API** (ADR-0019). There are no `resources` or `prompts` capabilities and
no `list_works`-style tools: an agent that wants to browse should use
this document's own endpoints.

Four verbs §71 names are **absent rather than stubbed** —
`search_releases`, `acquire_release`, `play_content` and
`transfer_playback`. Asking for one returns `-32601` with the milestone
that brings it, so an agent learns to wait rather than to retry. A tool
answering "not implemented" would be a published vocabulary with a hole
in it, which is exactly what ADR-0019 waited to avoid.

`sync_peer` was the fifth. It was deferred because the peer model held
exactly one peer and there was nothing to synchronise with; Milestone 4
stood up a second Full Peer, so it ships.

### §72

Controller-side MCP holds no key for encrypted personal state.
Playlists, ratings, reading positions and history are **not reachable
here** and no tool exposes them — asserted by enumerating the
registered surface, not by review.

200.description: The JSON-RPC response. Tool failures are errors INSIDE this envelope, not HTTP statuses.

202.description: A notification was accepted. No body.

get.summary: Report the peer identity this node derived from the client certificate.
get.description:
The peer the SERVER worked out, from the certificate presented on this
connection and the membership record pinning its key. Nothing in the
request asserts an identity and nothing is echoed back.

That is the whole reason the route exists. "The request returned 200"
is not evidence that pinning happened — a server that authenticated
nobody would also return 200 — so an acceptance assertion needs a value
it can compare against the id enrolment returned. This is that value.

It is served on the peer listener (`peer.listen`), which is off by
default: a deployment with one peer has no fabric to serve and needs no
certificate configuration of any kind.

200.description: The caller's membership record, as this node resolved it.

401.description:
No client certificate was presented. Behind the real listener this
is unreachable — the handshake is refused before a request exists —
and it is documented because the router refuses independently of
the listener it is mounted on.

403.description:
The presented key is not a member. It is the same answer for a key
that was never enrolled and a key that was revoked a moment ago:
after removal there is nothing left to tell them apart, which is
what "revocation is removing a membership record" means.

get.summary: Report whether this node can reach the peer that is asking.
get.description:
The RETURN leg of a pairing (#186, ADR-0040).

Replication needs traffic in both directions and the two flows run
opposite ways: a peer PUSHES its inventory to the controller, and a
destination PULLS bytes from a source (ADR-0030). On a one-way network
exactly one of them runs the wrong way, whichever node is the
destination, and replication deadlocks silently — a controller that was
never told a peer holds a blob correctly emits no work for it.

A node cannot observe the return direction for itself: an attempt that
never leaves the other machine leaves no trace here. So it asks, and
`heyarr peers add` consults this route to refuse a one-way pairing at
enrolment rather than leaving it to surface weeks later.

The request carries NOTHING. The address dialled is the answering
node's own membership record for the caller — never a target the caller
supplied, which would make every member a blind port scanner — and it
is also the address the return flows would really use.

200.description:
What the answering node observed. `unknown` is an ordinary answer,
not a failure: a node with no endpoint recorded for the caller has
nowhere to dial back to, and the caller must draw no conclusion
from it.

403.description: The presented key is not a member.

get.summary: Report this peer's attachment to the controller.
get.description:
A Full Peer is controller-attached: it runs no control plane and gets
its scheduling, authorisation and read routing from the controller
(ADR-0029). This is how it confirms which controller it is attached to
and what that controller records it as.

Every field is derived from the client certificate and the membership
record pinning its key (ADR-0033). There is no request body and no path
parameter, so nothing here can be influenced by the caller.

200.description: The caller's attachment, as this controller records it.

401.description:
No client certificate was presented. Behind the real listener this
is unreachable — the handshake is refused before a request exists.

403.description: The presented key is not a member.

post.summary: Attach to the controller, declaring which peer this node believes it is.
post.description:
The body carries a DECLARED `peer_id`. It is not a credential and it is
never the acting identity: the controller derives the acting peer from
the client certificate, compares the declaration against it, and
refuses a mismatch with 403 (ADR-0033).

The declaration is worth sending anyway. A peer restored from another
site's configuration, or pointed at the wrong data directory, finds out
on its first request rather than after an inventory report has landed
under somebody else's id.

It writes nothing. Attaching is a peer confirming what the controller
already holds; enrolment is an operator action on the admin surface,
and no peer credential can reach it.

200.description: The caller's attachment, as this controller records it.

400.description:
The body is not a JSON object, or carries no `peer_id`. The
declaration is required and is never defaulted to the certificate's
identity: a body that may be omitted is a body that stops being
compared.

403.description:
The presented key is not a member, or the declared `peer_id` is not
the peer this connection authenticated as. Peer A cannot act as
peer B.

post.summary: Report what this peer's content store actually holds.
post.description:
`replicas` is what the CONTROLLER believes. A peer's inventory is what
is on its DISK. Until a second Full Peer exists those two cannot
disagree — every writer of `replicas` resolves the self peer first, so
no row has ever described another machine — and this route is where
they get the chance to.

Disk reality wins (§21). The controller folds the report into
`replicas` as a cache of peer-reported reality: additions, changes,
and — the half that gets discovered late — **removals as `missing`,
never as deleted rows**. An inventory that could only add replicas
converges on a table that never shrinks and always claims the library
is safer than it is, and that table is what garbage collection consults
before deleting what it believes is a surplus copy.

The acting peer is derived from the client certificate. `peer_id` in
the body is a DECLARATION: it is compared against the certificate and a
mismatch is refused with 403 (ADR-0033). A peer reports its own
inventory and only its own.

### full vs incremental

The two differ in what they assert about a blob they do NOT mention:

* a **full** report names everything the peer holds, so an unmentioned
  blob is positively asserted absent — the row becomes `missing` and
  its `reported_at` advances, because the peer confirmed that blob by
  excluding it. This is the drift corrector: it is the only shape that
  can say "and nothing else".
* an **incremental** report asserts nothing about an unmentioned blob.
  The row is untouched and its `reported_at` does not advance. A loss
  is communicated with an explicit `missing` entry.

Both shapes of the same reality produce the same `replicas` state.

Reporting is idempotent (invariant 9): two identical consecutive
reports change nothing and emit no events.

200.description: What folding the report into `replicas` did.

400.description:
The body is not an inventory report, carries no `peer_id`, names an
unparseable blob hash or an unreportable state, or lists one blob
twice.

403.description:
The presented key is not a member, the declared `peer_id` is not
the peer this connection authenticated as, or the authenticated
peer has no catalog row to hang replicas from.

503.description:
This node has no catalog to record reports in. It answers rather
than accepting silently: a 200 would tell the peer its inventory
landed when nothing happened at all.

get.summary: Fetch this peer's materialised catalog snapshot.
get.description:
A Full Peer keeps a local materialised read snapshot of the
controller's catalogue so that it has something trustworthy to serve
from when the controller is not reachable (§52, §53). This is where it
comes from.

**The peer is the certificate's, always.** There is no peer id in the
path, the query or a body. A snapshot is a complete description of the
library's organisation, and a route that let a caller name a different
peer would both hand that peer's snapshot to any member and advance
that peer's version — so the real peer's next incremental refresh would
skip everything in between (ADR-0033).

**What it contains:** libraries, library roots, works, editions, blobs
and assets. Artwork references and known device access leases are §52
"potential contents" and are not here: leases are §54 and Milestone 7,
and there is no lease model yet.

**What it is not:** independently writable control state. The peer
materialises this into a SEPARATE database file with one writer and
read handles that cannot write; nothing a peer sends here writes
control state, and nothing it holds locally is control state
(ADR-0029, Invariant 5).

**Staleness is reported, not implied.** Every snapshot carries the
controller it came from, a monotonic version and when the catalogue was
read. A stale answer presented as current is worse than an unavailable
one, which is the whole shape of §53's "conservative rather than
unavailable".

parameters.name: holding
parameters.description:
The snapshot version this peer already has. Zero, or omitted, means
it has none — which is also what a peer whose snapshot store was
lost reports, and both correctly produce a full rebuild.

It is a CLAIM, not a credential. A peer claiming a version this
controller never issued gets a full rebuild rather than an
argument: the conservative answer to "we disagree about what you
have" is to send everything.

parameters.name: full
parameters.description:
Force the full rebuild even when an incremental refresh would be
legal. It is the drift corrector — the same escape hatch M4-07
gives inventory reporting — for when the snapshot and the catalogue
disagree and nobody can say why.

400.description: `holding` is not a non-negative integer.

post.summary: Push a backup of your OWN control plane to this peer (§50).
post.description:
A peer pushes a signed backup of its own control plane to the peers
that trust it, so that losing its disk is survivable (§50, ADR-0046).
Push, not pull: the bytes are the pusher's own small state, so ADR-0030's
"never carry content bytes" does not apply, and pushing moves the backup
structurally opposite the pulled catalog snapshot — one more way the two
artefacts cannot be confused.

**The source is the certificate's, always.** The manifest names the
source peer, and this node refuses a backup whose named source is not the
peer pushing it (ADR-0044 Q2): a peer may push only what it can sign as
itself, never another peer's control plane under its own name.

**Verified before it is stored.** The manifest signature is checked
against the pusher's pinned key, and the snapshot digest against its
bytes; a backup that fails either is rejected and nothing is stored. What
lands is inert — held in its own directory and never opened as a control
plane (Invariant 5, ADR-0044 Q5).

The manifest travels in the `X-Heyarr-Control-Backup` header (base64 JSON);
the request body is the snapshot database bytes.

parameters.name: X-Heyarr-Control-Backup
parameters.description: The base64-encoded JSON manifest of the pushed backup.

200.description: The backup was verified and stored.

400.description: The pushed backup was rejected (bad signature, digest mismatch, or a source that is not the caller).

503.description: This node does not hold control-plane backups for peers.

get.summary: What this peer holds of YOUR control plane (§50).
get.description:
Reports the generations this node holds of the CALLING peer's control
plane, newest first — the fact the pusher checks its own belief against
(ADR-0046). The peer is the certificate's; there is no id in the path or
query.

200.description: The generations held for the calling peer.

503.description: This node does not hold control-plane backups for peers.

get.summary: Fetch a generation of YOUR own backup this peer holds (§51).
get.description:
A recovering node fetches its own control-plane backup that this peer
holds, to rebuild its control plane (§51, M7-04, `recover --from-peer`).
The source is the certificate's, so a peer can download only ITS OWN
backups. The manifest is in the `X-Heyarr-Control-Backup` response header
(base64 JSON); the body is the snapshot database bytes. Generation `0`
means the latest held.

parameters.name: generation
parameters.description: The generation to fetch; 0 for the latest held.

200.description: The backup bundle — manifest in the header, snapshot in the body.

400.description: The generation is not a non-negative integer.

404.description: No such backup is held for the calling peer.

503.description: This node does not hold control-plane backups for peers.

get.summary: This peer's access leases, for a sibling to cache (§54, ADR-0048).
get.description:
Returns the signed access-lease tokens this peer has issued and that are
still live — unrevoked, and unexpired on this peer's clock — so a sibling
can cache them and, once this peer is unreachable, still answer a read on
whose authority (§53, §54, #285).

**The tokens carry their own authority.** Each is a capability grant
(ADR-0048) signed by this peer's identity key; a fetching peer verifies
it against the key it already pinned for this one (ADR-0012), never
against the connection that served it — a lease served by A stays A's
signed statement however it travelled (the ADR-0043 caution). Serving
them to a member therefore discloses nothing a member could not be
granted, which is why the route needs no authorisation beyond membership.

200.description: The signed tokens of this peer's active leases (possibly empty).

503.description: This node issues no access leases to cache.

get.summary: The editorial catalog op log, for a sibling to converge (§49, ADR-0073).
get.description:
Returns every editorial catalog op this node holds — the signed
delete/restore ops the two sites of an active-active pair converge on so
one site does not rebuild a work the other logically deleted (ADR-0073,
#449). A sibling merges them into its own log; the set is a G-set, so the
merge is order-independent and idempotent.

**Each op carries its own authority.** An op is signed by the peer that
issued it (ADR-0012) and re-verified on every evaluation; a sibling
checks it against the key it already pinned, never against the connection
that served it. Serving them to a member therefore discloses nothing a
member could not already read, which is why the route needs no
authorisation beyond membership.

200.description: The op tokens this node holds (possibly empty).

503.description: This node does not converge a catalog with a sibling.

post.summary: Push editorial catalog ops, and receive the merged log (§49, ADR-0073).
post.description:
Records the catalog ops a sibling pushes and answers with this node's
full log, so one exchange converges both directions: the pushed ops land
here and the response carries anything the pusher was missing. The G-set
makes this safe to repeat — recording is idempotent by op hash, and an op
whose signature does not verify is refused with 400 without recording any
op in the batch.

200.description: The merged op set this node now holds (possibly empty).

400.description: A pushed op did not verify, or the body was malformed.

503.description: This node does not converge a catalog with a sibling.

parameters.name: space
parameters.description: The opaque space id (a UUIDv7).

get.summary: A space's causal heads, offered for incremental sync (§42, §44, ADR-0049).
get.description:
Returns the space's causal frontier — the change ids no other change
names as a parent. A sibling offers its own heads and pulls only what it
is missing beneath them, never a full-log replay (the resumable sync a
phone needs, §46). A head is an opaque change id; nothing here is
decrypted (Invariant 6). This is a SEPARATE protocol from CAS sync (§44)
that shares this listener and its mTLS authentication.

404.description: This peer does not hold that encrypted space.

503.description: This node keeps no encrypted personal state to sync.

parameters.name: space
parameters.description: The opaque space id (a UUIDv7).

get.summary: The opaque changes a caller is missing — ciphertext only (§42, §44).
get.description:
Serves the space's encrypted changes. A caller may offer its known heads
as repeated `have` query parameters; only the changes it is missing
beneath this peer's frontier are then returned (pure DAG reachability, no
decryption). With no `have`, the whole set is served. Every change is
opaque: a content-addressed id, its causal parents, and ciphertext the
peer never decrypted.

parameters.name: have
parameters.description: A causal head the caller already holds; repeat for each.

200.description: The changes the caller is missing (possibly empty), as ciphertext.

404.description: This peer does not hold that encrypted space.

503.description: This node keeps no encrypted personal state to sync.

post.summary: Accept one opaque change; the peer verifies its content-address (§42, Invariant 1).
post.description:
Accepts one encrypted change from a sibling. The peer re-derives the
change's blake3 id over its space, parents and ciphertext and refuses a
mismatch (it never trusts a claimed id), then stores the ciphertext
without decrypting it. Idempotent on the id.

200.description: The id the peer verified and stored the change under.

400.description: The change is malformed or its id does not match its bytes.

404.description: This peer does not hold that encrypted space.

503.description: This node keeps no encrypted personal state to sync.

parameters.name: space
parameters.description: The opaque space id (a UUIDv7).

get.summary: The newest opaque snapshot a space holds — ciphertext only (§44).
get.description:
Offers the latest encrypted snapshot this peer holds for a space, so a
replicating sibling can seed a bounded snapshot + tail rather than the
whole change log. The snapshot is opaque: a content-addressed id, its
causal frontier, and ciphertext the peer never decrypted. 404 when the
space is held but has no snapshot yet, or is not held at all.

404.description: This peer holds no snapshot for that space (or does not hold the space).

503.description: This node keeps no encrypted personal state to sync.

parameters.name: space
parameters.description: The opaque space id (a UUIDv7).

post.summary: Accept one opaque snapshot; the peer verifies its content-address (§44, Invariant 1).
post.description:
Accepts one encrypted snapshot from a sibling. The peer re-derives the
snapshot's blake3 id over its space, frontier and ciphertext and refuses a
mismatch, then stores the ciphertext without decrypting it. Idempotent on
the id.

200.description: The id the peer verified and stored the snapshot under.

400.description: The snapshot is malformed or its id does not match its bytes.

404.description: This peer does not hold that encrypted space.

503.description: This node keeps no encrypted personal state to sync.

parameters.name: space
parameters.description: The opaque space id (a UUIDv7).

post.summary: Replicate a space's identity to a Full Peer (§37, §45).
post.description:
A replicating sibling records a space's opaque id and its structural kind
on this peer, so a Full Peer holds the whole encrypted space alongside the
wrapped keys and changes. Idempotent; a space already held is a no-op.

204.description: The space is recorded (or was already held).

400.description: The kind is unknown.

503.description: This node keeps no encrypted personal state to sync.

parameters.name: space
parameters.description: The opaque space id (a UUIDv7).

post.summary: Replicate a wrapped copy of a space's key to a Full Peer (§41, §45).
post.description:
A replicating sibling pushes one recipient's sealed copy of a space's key.
The bytes are opaque — the peer holds them and cannot open them.
Idempotent per (space, recipient); a re-push replaces the copy.

recipient.description: The recipient encryption key this copy is sealed for (x25519:<hex>).

204.description: The wrapped key is stored (or replaced).

400.description: The recipient or wrapped bytes are empty.

404.description: This peer does not hold that encrypted space.

503.description: This node keeps no encrypted personal state to sync.

parameters.name: hash
parameters.description: The BLAKE3 digest that names the blob, as `blake3:<64 lowercase hex characters>`.

get.summary: Serve a blob's bytes to a pinned peer, whole or by range.
get.description:
**The byte-carrying hop.** This is the connection a replica actually
travels over: the destination opens it, reads these bytes and verifies
them against its own expectation (§21, ADR-0030). The controller is not
on this path and there is no route anywhere that would put it there —
no redirect, no proxy, no "just for the first sync" special case (§32).
The controller schedules and authorises; it never carries bytes.

It is the **same handler** as `/api/v1/blobs/{hash}/content`, which
ADR-0013 called out in advance: blob serving is a contract, not an
endpoint, and a replication-specific copy would be a second range
implementation to keep in step. Ranges, the strong `ETag`, immutable
caching and flat memory use are therefore identical here.

What differs is the credential, which is why this is a separate route
rather than the same one. The client API authenticates a bearer token
(ADR-0011) and a peer holds none; this surface authenticates a pinned
Ed25519 key in a client certificate (ADR-0012). Membership **is** the
authorisation: a pinned member may read any blob this deployment holds,
because a Full Peer's desired blob set is the complete canonical set
(§19) and denying it individual blobs would be vacuous.

The source makes no decision about what the destination needs. It
serves an ordinary blob read.

parameters.name: download
parameters.description: `1`, `true` or `yes` adds `Content-Disposition: attachment`. The bytes, ranges and validators are identical either way.

ETag.description: `"blake3-<hex digest>"`. A destination never verifies against this: it hashes what arrives and compares against the digest it asked for. Trusting the validator would be trusting the source with extra steps (invariant 1).

400.description: The path is not a `blake3:<64 hex>` digest.

403.description: The presented key is not a member of this fabric.

404.description:
This peer holds no such blob. Distinct from 503: a destination
reads this as "try another source".

416.description: The requested range lies outside the blob.

503.description:
This node has no content store behind its peer surface, so it is
not serving bytes at all. Distinct from 404: there is nothing here
to try again for.

head.summary: Report a blob's size and range support without transferring it.
head.description: Identical to `get` in every header, with no body. §28 makes it part of the contract every peer advertises.

200.description: The blob exists; `Content-Length` is its size.

400.description: The path is not a `blake3:<64 hex>` digest.

403.description: The presented key is not a member of this fabric.

404.description: This peer holds no such blob.

503.description: This node has no content store behind its peer surface.

parameters.name: hash
parameters.description: The BLAKE3 digest that names the BLOB, as `blake3:<64 lowercase hex characters>`. A manifest is looked up by the identity of the bytes it describes and is never itself an address, so there is deliberately no route anywhere that names a manifest by its own digest (ADR-0034).

get.summary: Describe a blob's chunk sequence to a pinned peer.
get.description:
**A description, not a negotiation.** The destination fetches what the
source stored and decides for itself what to do about it (§20, §21,
ADR-0030). This route is never told what the destination holds, is
never asked what it should send, and computes no difference: there is
no request body, no query parameter, and no response field that varies
with the caller, so two peers asking about one blob get byte-identical
answers. Anything else would make the source a participant in a
decision it cannot verify, and would put the destination's inventory on
the wire for no reason.

**Asking never generates.** There is no manifest-on-demand here and
there will not be. A `GET` that chunked a blob to answer would be a
remote denial of service with a polite name — one request naming a
20 GB blob, and the source reads 20 GB off its disks. §16 makes
chunking lazy and ADR-0034 makes a manifest discardable at any moment,
so "there is no manifest" is a legitimate, permanent state and the
`404` below is the **answer**. A destination that receives it pulls the
blob whole from `/peer/v1/blobs/{hash}/content`, which is exactly
Milestone 4's behaviour and is always correct.

**The credential is the same one.** Mounted beside the content route,
on the same mTLS trust root (ADR-0012), with no new credential and no
per-blob capability: a pinned member may already read the bytes this
manifest describes, so refusing it the description would be theatre.

**The digest names the manifest.** `digest` is the manifest's own
content address, so a destination can check it received the manifest
the source has. It is not an alias for the blob, nothing resolves it to
bytes, and the destination still verifies the whole-object digest
itself on any transfer that follows (ADR-0034).

**`chunks` is a sequence, not a set.** The order is the data: a set of
individually valid chunks assembled in the wrong order is a set of
valid chunks and the wrong file. `digest` covers the chunk digests in
index order for exactly that reason, so a shuffled array produces a
response the destination rejects rather than one it reassembles
wrongly.

200.description: The stored manifest, its chunks in index order.

400.description: The path is not a `blake3:<64 hex>` digest.

403.description: The presented key is not a member of this fabric.

404.description:
Two distinct answers, told apart by the problem document's `type`
URI — never by its prose, which is expected to be reworded — and
the destination takes a different action on each.

`.../problems/no-chunk-manifest`: this node **holds** the blob and
has no chunk manifest for it. Asking does not produce one. Pull
these bytes whole from this same source.

`.../problems/not-found`: this node holds no such blob at all.
There is nothing to read here whole or in chunks; try another
source.

503.description:
This node has no content store behind its peer surface, so it is
not serving bytes at all and has no manifests to describe them
with. Matches the content route: distinct from 404 because there is
nothing here to try again for.

parameters.name: hash
parameters.description: The BLAKE3 digest that names the blob, as `blake3:<64 lowercase hex characters>`. Pieces are not addressable and never will be: a piece is a transport detail with a session's lifetime, not a name for bytes (ADR-0041), so there is deliberately no route that names one.

get.summary: Report which pieces of a blob this node holds.
get.description:
**The question replication could never ask.** Every other route here
answers about a blob held WHOLE — the inventory lists them, the content
route serves them, the manifest describes them. A peer holding part of
a blob was indistinguishable from one holding none of it, so two peers
both still fetching the same blob had nothing to say to each other and
the only available shape was `Internet → A`, then `A → B` (§23).

This is the third answer: *I have some of it, and here is which.*

**Asking never computes.** The piece geometry is derived from the
blob's SIZE, which this node already knows, so answering never reads a
byte of content. That is what makes the route safe behind a credential
any pinned member holds — the same reasoning ADR-0034 applies to
refusing manifest-on-demand, arriving at the opposite conclusion
because the cost here is genuinely zero.

**The answer is a claim, not evidence.** A peer saying it holds a piece
is a peer saying so. The destination verifies every piece it receives
against that piece's hash, and the whole object against its BLAKE3
digest before it becomes a blob (invariant 1). A peer that overstates
wastes one request and is walked past, exactly as a source that serves
bytes it cannot back is walked past by repair (ADR-0036).

**The credential is the same one.** Mounted beside the content and
manifest routes on the same mTLS trust root (ADR-0012), with no new
credential and no per-blob capability: a pinned member may already read
these bytes, and telling it which of them are here reveals nothing it
could not discover by asking for them.

200.description:
What this node holds of the blob. `available` carries the blob's
SIZE so that a peer computing a different geometry is refused
rather than half-believed: two peers requesting pieces whose
boundaries they do not share produce bytes that fail verification
for a reason nobody could diagnose (ADR-0043).

400.description: The path is not a `blake3:<64 hex>` digest.

403.description: The presented key is not a member of this fabric.

404.description:
This node holds no part of the blob and has no transfer of it in
progress. Distinct from a `200` carrying an empty `available`,
which would mean a transfer that has landed nothing yet — the
difference between *never heard of it* and *fetching, nothing yet*,
which are different things to a session choosing sources.

503.description:
This node has no content store behind its peer surface, so it holds
no pieces to report. Matches the content and manifest routes:
distinct from 404 because there is nothing here to try again for.

parameters.name: hash
parameters.description: The BLAKE3 digest that names the blob.

parameters.name: index
parameters.description: The piece's index in the division the blob's size implies, as reported by the availability route. Indices are meaningful only within that geometry and are not names for bytes (ADR-0041).

get.summary: Serve one piece of a blob, held whole or in part.
get.description:
**Why this is a route and not a `Range` header.** ADR-0042 said
fetching a piece would be a ranged `GET` against the existing content
route, and for a blob held WHOLE that is exactly right. It does not
work for a blob held in PART, which is the case §23 exists for. The
content route promises the blob: a strong `ETag` naming the
whole-object digest, a `Content-Length` that is the blob's length, and
a `404` meaning *this peer does not have it*. A node holding a third of
the bytes can honour none of those, and making it try would mean either
lying about the `ETag` or inventing partial-content semantics on a
route whose contract is deliberately simple (ADR-0013).

So this route is the one way a piece is fetched, from a whole blob and
a partial one alike, and the content route is left exactly as it is for
the whole-blob pulls replication already does.

**The bitset gates it.** A piece the availability record does not claim
is refused even when the staging file happens to have bytes at that
offset, because a partial's length is a high-water mark: bytes may be
present at an offset whose piece was never completed. This is the one
place where believing the bitset wrongly sends bad bytes to somebody
else rather than failing locally (ADR-0043).

**No validator.** A piece is not addressable, so an `ETag` would be a
cache key for a thing with a session's lifetime, and a peer that cached
it would later serve a piece of a geometry that no longer applies.

400.description: The hash is not a `blake3:<64 hex>` digest, or the index is not a non-negative integer.

403.description: The presented key is not a member of this fabric.

404.description:
This node does not hold that piece — it knows nothing of the blob,
or its availability does not claim that index, or the index is past
the end of the blob's division. All three are the same answer to
the caller: try another peer, or ask again later. This is the
ordinary answer while two peers converge, not a fault.

503.description: This node has no content store behind its peer surface.

get.summary: Page the quality profiles.
get.description: Ordered by `name`, which is unique.

post.summary: Author a quality profile.
post.description:
A **create, not an upsert**. Device registration is an upsert because a
television announces itself on every launch and nobody chose to do it;
a profile is authored deliberately, and silently replacing one because
the name matched would discard whatever it said before. A name
collision is a `409`.

Rules are validated here, at write time — an attribute that does not
exist, an ordering comparison on a codec name, or a weight on a gate is
a `400` naming the section and the rule. That is deliberate: a mistake
in a profile should be reported to whoever wrote the profile, not
turned into a rejection reason attached to every candidate for the next
six months.

409.description: A profile with that name already exists.

get.summary: One quality profile.

put.description:
A section the request **omits** is left alone; a section sent as `[]`
is **cleared**. Those are different intentions, and collapsing them
would make "clear this profile's terminal rules" and "forget to send
them" the same request.

A request that changes nothing emits no event. A client that re-sends
its whole configuration on every start would otherwise turn the event
stream into a heartbeat.

200.description: The profile as it now stands.

409.description: The new name is already taken.

delete.description:
Physical, not logical — a deliberate departure from ADR-0018's stance
for *content*. ADR-0018 is about bytes: deleting an asset must not
unlink blobs inline because bytes are expensive, shared and
unrecoverable. A profile is a page of configuration, cheap to retype
and referenced by nothing but desired state, and a soft-deleted one
would have to be filtered out of every read path forever to avoid an
operator seeing a profile they deleted.

A profile still referenced by desired state is refused with `409`
rather than cascaded: deleting the standard by which desire is
measured, and leaving the desire, would make satisfaction unanswerable.

post.summary: Score release candidates against a profile, and explain every answer.
post.description:
§63: evaluation is **deterministic and inspectable**. This endpoint is
what makes the second half true — an evaluation you can only reach
through a background job is not inspectable, because "why did it pick
that release, last Tuesday, at 3am" cannot be answered by re-running
something that has since moved on.

It **writes nothing**. A `POST` because the body carries the
candidates, not because it changes anything — the same reasoning as
`/playback/plan` — and it needs only `read`.

Hand it candidates and it answers with the same values the search job
will get, which makes a profile testable *before* it is used in anger.

### The reasons are the deliverable

Every rule that was considered produces a reason, not only the ones
that failed — a rule that ran silently is a rule nobody can confirm
ran. §61 lists opaque scoring among the things Heyarr avoids, and a
score with no reasons is exactly that.

| result | meaning |
|---|---|
| `pass` | an `accept` or `terminal` rule held |
| `fail` | an `accept` rule did not hold — **this gate rejected the candidate**, and nothing else uses this word |
| `bonus` / `penalty` | a `prefer` rule landed, contributing its (possibly negative) weight |
| `miss` | a `prefer` rule did not land, or a `terminal` condition was not reached. **Not** a rejection |
| `undetermined` | the provider could not determine the attribute |

`undetermined` is deliberately not `fail`. "This release is 720p and
you wanted 1080p" and "nobody could tell what resolution this is" are
different situations, and an operator seeing the second knows to look
at the provider rather than at the release. An undetermined **gate**
still rejects — a gate that cannot be shown to hold must not pass, or a
profile saying "1080p minimum" quietly accepts a release nobody could
measure.

### The ranking is a total order

Accepted candidates rank above rejected ones (a rejected candidate's
score is a number about something that will not be used); then by score
descending; then by **candidate id ascending**, which is a stable key
that does not depend on the order the candidates were supplied in.

Without that last tie-break two equally good releases swap places
between runs and the upgrade workflow churns between them forever — a
bug that presents as bandwidth.

`selected` is a separate field rather than "the first of `ranked`"
because the first element is not necessarily acceptable: when
everything was rejected it is merely the least bad, and acquiring it
would be exactly what §62's gates exist to prevent.

get.summary: Page the job queue.
One job.

post.summary: Put a finished job back on the queue. Requires `write`.
post.description:
An operator action: something was wrong and has been fixed. Only a
succeeded, failed or dead job may be retried; a pending or leased one is
a 409, because "retry" on a job that is already running would mean
running it twice.

get.summary: The event stream (server-sent events).
get.description:
A live SSE feed of §76 events, preceded by everything after `after`.

Reconnection is gapless: a client that saw sequence N reconnects with
`?after=N` and receives everything since, with no hole and no duplicate.
The subscription is opened before the catch-up read — the other order
leaves a window in which committed events are in neither half, and both
halves look complete on their own.

Each frame carries `id: <seq>`, so a browser `EventSource` resumes on
its own via `Last-Event-ID`, which this endpoint honours when `after` is
absent.

A slow consumer is dropped rather than backpressured (ADR-0009). When
that happens the stream emits one `heyarr.stream.gap` event carrying
`resume_after` and `dropped`, and closes. Reconnect with
`?after=resume_after`. Closing silently would be indistinguishable from
a network blip, and a client cannot tell "refill" from "carry on".

Resume from the highest sequence number you have seen. Under concurrent
writes a straggler may arrive slightly out of order; nothing is ever
delivered twice.

parameters.name: after
parameters.description: Deliver everything with a sequence number greater than this.

parameters.name: types
parameters.description:
Comma-separated event types. Each is an exact name (`job.failed`) or
a trailing-`*` namespace prefix (`job.*`).

get.summary: Every pinned user identity. Requires `admin`.
get.description:
The device-identity trust root (§40, ADR-0048): the user public keys
this node has pinned, against which a device's enrolment cert is
verified. Reading it is `admin` because the list is a map of who may
authenticate as a principal on this node. It carries no secret and no
cert — a user identity's private key is the person's and never enters
the server (ADR-0032).

post.summary: Pin a user identity. Requires `admin`.
post.description:
The out-of-band pin ADR-0032 requires: an operator reads a user's public
key from `heyarr identity show` and posts it here. Nothing that user
signs is honoured until this pin exists — "a key issued and immediately
honoured" must stay unspellable, so pinning is a deliberate human act,
not something a device can assert about itself.

public_key.description: The user's public key, `ed25519:<64 hex characters>`.

recovery_encryption_key.description: The identity's X25519 recovery encryption PUBLIC key, `x25519:<hex>` (§41, ADR-0049). Registered here so the device-enrolment response can carry it to an enrolling device, which wraps new personal-state spaces for recovery. A public recipient only — the paper recovery SECRET never enters the server. Optional; omit for an identity with none.

delete.description:
Revocation is removing the pin (ADR-0012's shape, applied to a user). It
cascades to the user's devices: a device authenticates only as its user,
and a device with no user authenticates as nobody. Returns the record it
removed rather than 204, so an operator can see exactly which key stopped
being trusted.

get.summary: A user's enrolled devices. Requires `admin`.
get.description:
The device keys this user has vouched for. The enrolment cert is not on
the wire: authentication re-verifies the presented cert against the
pinned user key rather than trusting a stored copy, so the stored token
is an implementation detail, not a field a client reads.

post.summary: Enrol a device under the user its cert names. Requires `admin`.
post.description:
The cert is the whole request: it names its own user and device keys and
is verified against the pinned user key before anything is written, so a
device cannot be enrolled under a user who did not sign for it, and a
cert naming an unpinned user is refused.

cert.description: The user-signed enrolment cert, as `heyarr identity enrol` produced.

delete.description:
A tombstone, unlike a user revoke: the row stays and `revoked_at` is set,
so a re-presented cert for the key is refused rather than silently
re-enrolled, and the revocation is auditable.

get.summary: Every credential. Requires `admin`.
get.description:
Not paginated: the number of tokens is the number of integrations an
operator has set up, and unlike the catalog nothing writes to this table
while it is being read.

200.description: The credentials. Never any secret material.

post.summary: Mint a credential. Requires `admin`.

201.description:
The credential and its secret. The secret is returned exactly once
and is not recoverable: only its argon2id hash was stored.

get.summary: One credential. Requires `admin`.

delete.description:
Logical: the row stays and `revoked_at` is set. An audit trail that
deletes the thing being audited is not one. Revoking twice is a 409, so
a script cannot mistake "already revoked" for "revoked something just
now".

bearerAuth.description:
An opaque scoped token (ADR-0011), presented as `Authorization: Bearer
heyarr_…`. The header is the only place a credential is accepted: a
`?token=` parameter would write it into every proxy log, browser history
and Referer header between the client and here.

Scopes are ordered — `admin` implies `write` implies `read`. Every
route under /api/v1 requires at least `read`.

peerCertificate.description:
A self-signed X.509 certificate carrying this peer's Ed25519 public
key, pinned against the controller-issued membership record
(ADR-0012). There is no CA and no PKI: the certificate proves
possession of a key, and membership decides whether that key may
speak. Both ends pin, so the dialler authenticates the listener by
exactly the same rule.

It is checked twice — during the handshake, and again on every request
the connection carries. Revocation is deleting the membership record,
and there is no revocation list to fall back on, so the freshness of
that second lookup is the mechanism.

This credential is accepted ONLY on /peer/v1, and a bearer token is
never accepted there. A connection presenting no client certificate is
refused during the handshake, not with a status code.

publicKey.name: key
publicKey.description:
A rendered Ed25519 public key, `ed25519:<64 hex characters>` — a user
key on the user routes, a device key on the device route. The ":" is a
legal path character and no key contains a "/".

cursor.name: cursor
cursor.description:
An opaque position from a previous page's `next_cursor`. It is scoped to
one collection: a cursor from `/works` is rejected by `/jobs` rather
than being read as a position in a different sort order.

limit.name: limit
limit.description: Values above the maximum are clamped, not rejected.

BadRequest.description: The request is malformed or semantically invalid.

Unauthorized.description: No credential, or one that was rejected.

Forbidden.description: A valid credential that does not carry the required scope.

NotFound.description:
No such resource. Never an empty 200: a client cannot tell "no such
work" from "a work with nothing in it" if both are 200, and it is the
difference between retrying and giving up.

SelfEnrolledDevice.description: A device as this peer now knows it, after self-enrolment (ADR-0067).

encryption_key.description: The device's X25519 encryption key, `x25519:<hex>`, when the cert binds one.

recovery_encryption_key.description: The user identity's X25519 recovery encryption PUBLIC key, `x25519:<hex>` (§41, ADR-0049; rarebit-one/heyarr-mobile#41). Carried so the enrolling device can wrap new personal-state spaces for recovery from the moment it enrols. A public recipient — only the paper recovery secret decrypts, and that secret never transits. Absent when the identity has none.

user.description: The pinned user the device is enrolled under, `ed25519:<hex>`.

admitted_by.description: The hash (`sha256:<hex>`) of the op that admitted the device — what the device cites as its own admission (ADR-0068).

expires_at.description: When the admitting op expires; any member may re-add the device before then.

Membership.description: An identity's membership op log as this node holds it (ADR-0068).

ops.description: Every recorded op token, oldest issued first. Empty is `[]`, never null.

recorded.description: On a push, how many of the posted ops this node had not seen. Absent on a GET.

EncryptedSpace.description:
A personal-state space as the peer holds it (§38, §39). Opaque id,
structural kind, and when the peer recorded it — never a name.

WrappedKeyInput.description: One recipient's sealed copy of a space key, as pushed at create time.

recipient.description: The recipient encryption key this copy is sealed for (x25519:<hex>).

wrapped.description: The opaque sealed bytes (base64). The peer cannot open them.

PlacementPinInput.description: An opaque placement pin (ADR-0096): a ciphertext vault blob and the peer it should live on. The pin is identified by this pair — there is no server-minted id — so the same shape records a pin (POST) and removes it (DELETE).

blob_hash.description: The BLAKE3 digest naming the ciphertext blob, as `blake3:<64 lowercase hex characters>`.

peer_id.description: The peer the blob should live on. Not checked for existence — a pin may outlive churn in peers.

WrappedKey.description: A stored wrapped copy of a space key.

EncryptedChange.description:
One opaque CRDT change (§42, §44). Content-addressed by the blake3 digest
of its space, parents and ciphertext; the peer verifies the id and never
decrypts the ciphertext.

change_id.description: blake3:<hex> over space, parents and ciphertext.

ciphertext.description: The encrypted change (base64), opaque to the peer.

EncryptedSnapshot.description:
A materialised CRDT state at a causal point (§44), encrypted under the
space key. Content-addressed by the blake3 digest of its space, frontier
and ciphertext; the peer verifies the id and never decrypts it.

snapshot_id.description: blake3:<hex> over space, frontier and ciphertext.

frontier.description: The causal heads this snapshot materialises; the tail begins after them.

ciphertext.description: The encrypted materialised state (base64), opaque to the peer.

Problem.description: RFC 9457. Clients branch on `type` and nothing else.

request_id.description: Correlates the response with the server log line.

work_key.description: Normalised identity, so a rescan converges on the same work.

attributes.description:
Per-content-type fields. They live here rather than as columns so
that registering a fourth content type is not a migration.

ExternalIDs.description:
The identifiers this entity is known by outside heyarr, keyed by source
(`tmdb`, `imdb`, `tvdb`) — ADR-0050's REST twin, read-only (#431).
`{}` when nothing has been reconciled: an absent identifier is "no
match", never an error (ADR-0025).

Where the catalog holds more than one identifier for one source, the
lexically-first value is reported — an arbitrary but STABLE answer,
the same determinism rule `/search`'s `tvdb_id` takes.

WorkDetail.description:
A work with its external identifiers and its browse embeds (ADR-0075).
Returned by `GET /works/{id}`. The embeds are always present here —
one row, two cheap lookups — and `null` when the work has none.

WorkCard.description:
A listing row with the browse embeds `include=` asked for (ADR-0075).
An embed not asked for is absent from the object; one asked for that
the work lacks is `null`. Those are different answers — "I did not
ask" and "there is no poster".

GroupSummary.description:
One artist or author (ADR-0075): a grouping over works keyed by the
name the identifier wrote, never an entity with an id.

artwork.description: The cover of the group's first work (by year, then title), or null.

ArtworkRef.description:
A work's representative poster (ADR-0075): the `artwork`-role asset
that ranks first — `poster`/`cover`/`folder`/`front` before an unnamed
image before `fanart`/`backdrop`/`banner` — among those that hold
bytes and are not missing. `content_url` is the ordinary blob route
(ADR-0013); `GET /works/{id}/artwork` redirects to the same place.

mime.description: The asset's recorded media type; the blob route itself declares octet-stream.

PrimaryAssetRef.description:
The one file a card tap plays (ADR-0075): the first `primary`-role
asset of the work that holds bytes and is not missing — an arbitrary
but stable choice among a work's editions. Enough to hand to
`POST /playback/plan` or the blob route without a second read; a
client that wants to choose lists `GET /works/{id}/assets`.

duration_seconds.description: From the blob's probe when one has been taken, else null.

EditionDetail.description: An edition with its external identifiers. Returned by `GET /editions/{id}`.

WorkPatch.description:
The catalogue facts an operator may correct on a work (#428). Every
field is optional; an omitted field is left alone.

title.description: Stored as typed (trimmed). Blank is refused.

year.description: `0` clears the year, which is not the same as omitting the field.

content_type.description: Must be a content type this node knows.

blob_hash.description:
Null for a `linked` asset, which has no blob at all — not a mutable
one, not a special one, none (ADR-0020). That is what keeps blob
immutability absolute.

missing_since.description: Set when the source path vanished. Not a deletion.

WorkAsset.description:
An asset of a work, with its edition labelled and its blob's facts
inlined (#429).

blob_size.description:
Null for a `linked` asset, which has no blob at all (ADR-0020) —
the same null `blob_hash` carries.

chunked.description: Compatibility only: true exactly when `chunk_manifest` is `present`. It was a stored column from Milestone 1 until migration 00029 and was `false` on every row in every deployment, because nothing ever wrote it. It is now computed, and it is kept rather than removed because it is a required field and dropping it would break every client that reads it. It cannot express the third state §16 needs, so do not branch on it — read `chunk_manifest`.

chunk_manifest.description: Whether these bytes have a chunk manifest (§15, §16, ADR-0034). `present` — one exists. `not_required` — a decision was recorded that these bytes will never need one; §16 allows that small blobs never do. `undecided` — nobody has decided yet. The last two are what a single boolean could not tell apart, and they are the two a replication decision branches on. Reading this field never causes a manifest to be generated.

site.description: The failure domain this peer is in.

endpoint.description:
Where to reach the peer — an `https` origin, or a `unix://`
socket path — or null when no endpoint is recorded. A
bare `host:port` given at registration is stored as
`https://host:port`. Not its identity.

public_key.description:
The peer's Ed25519 identity as `ed25519:<64 lowercase hex>` — the
same algorithm-prefixed shape as a blob digest, so the two are not
confused in a terminal. Null for a peer that has not established an
identity yet (ADR-0012).

This is the PUBLIC half, and it is what another site needs in order
to enrol this peer. The private key is never exposed here or
anywhere else in the API: it is a 0600 file in the data directory
that the API layer does not read.

enrolled_at.description:
When this peer was admitted to the fabric (M4-04). For the self
peer it equals `created_at`. Revocation is deletion (ADR-0012), so
a peer removed and re-enrolled comes back with a new `id` and a new
`enrolled_at` — which is what makes this the answer to "has
membership changed?" rather than a copy of `created_at`.

health.description:
Whether this peer is reachable (§31, §32, M4-10).

It is OBSERVED, not declared. A peer is `reachable` because it
answered something recently — an inventory report, a served range,
or a cheap probe when nothing else has happened — and there is no
endpoint through which a peer can assert its own health.

`unreachable` means SILENCE past the window, not a failed request.
A peer that answered a request with a 500 is `reachable`: a 500
proves a process is listening, and the question here is whether
anything is there. `unknown` is a peer nothing has ever heard from,
and it is deliberately not a synonym for reachable — an unprobed
peer has not been shown to be up.

Health is advisory for reads and does not affect membership: an
unreachable peer is skipped as a read source, and still accrues the
replication work it is owed.

last_seen_at.description:
When this peer last answered anything, or null if it never has.

It ships beside `health` rather than instead of it because
"unreachable" on its own is a status nobody can act on: it does not
say whether to go and restart something or to wait twenty seconds.

snapshot.description:
The peer's materialised catalog snapshot (§52, M4-13), or `null`
when this controller has never issued it one.

Explicitly nullable rather than an omitted key, and never a zero
object. "This peer holds a snapshot of an empty library" and "this
peer holds no snapshot" are different answers — in Milestone 7 one
means the library is empty and the other means the peer cannot help
you — and a client that had to tell them apart by inspecting a row
count would eventually get it wrong during an outage, which is the
only time it matters.

PeerSnapshot.description:
What a peer's catalog snapshot is a fact ABOUT: which controller, which
version, and how old (§52, §53).

controller_id.description:
The controller whose catalogue this is. Recorded even though there
is exactly one controller (ADR-0029), because a snapshot restored
from another deployment's backup (§51, §82) has to be recognisable
as somebody else's.

version.description:
Monotonic per peer, allocated by the controller — the single writer
is the only place monotonicity can actually be guaranteed
(ADR-0003). It starts at 1; there is no version 0, because absent
is the absence of a snapshot rather than a snapshot numbered zero.

generated_at.description:
When the controller READ the catalogue — not when the peer applied
it, and not when a row was last written.

kind.description:
Which path produced this one. A full rebuild is the drift
corrector, and "when did this peer last take the slow, safe path?"
is an operational question that is unanswerable if the two are
indistinguishable after the fact.

rows.description: How many rows it carries, across every covered table.

content_digest.description:
A fingerprint of the CONTENTS, excluding the metadata — so an
incremental refresh and a full rebuild of the same catalogue state
can be shown to be identical, which they are.

age_seconds.description:
How old the snapshot is, measured against the CONTROLLER's clock,
which is the only clock that can say how stale its own catalogue
read is. It may be negative if the reader's clock is behind; that
is reported as measured rather than clamped, because an operator
who sees a negative age has learned something true.

PeerBlobPieces.description:
What one node holds of a blob, whole or in part (§23, ADR-0042,
ADR-0043).

It is a CLAIM and never evidence. Every piece a destination receives is
verified against that piece's hash, and the whole object against its
BLAKE3 digest before it becomes a blob (invariant 1), so a node that
overstates costs one wasted request and cannot cause a wrong blob.

blob_hash.description: The blob asked about, echoed so a response cannot be mistaken for one about a different blob if it is logged or cached.

available.description:
The availability, as `<blob size in bytes>:<lowercase hex bitset>`,
one bit per piece in index order.

The SIZE is what is on the wire, and neither the piece count nor
the piece length is. The count cannot be implied by the bitset's
width — a bitset for 20 pieces and one for 21 are both three bytes
— and the count in turn does not determine the piece length: 1024
pieces is a 256 MiB blob at 256 KiB pieces and equally an 8 GiB
blob at 8 MiB pieces. The size determines both, by the same
deterministic rule both peers already run, so the reader derives
the geometry rather than believing a claimed one, and a peer
describing a division this node would not compute is refused
(ADR-0043).

An empty string means this node holds none of it yet — a transfer
in progress that has landed nothing. A node that knows nothing
about the blob answers `404` instead.

PeerBlobManifest.description:
One blob's chunk sequence, as a source describes it to a pinned peer
(§15, §16, ADR-0034).

It is an optimisation and never an identity. It is keyed by
`blob_hash`, the ADR-0005 whole-object digest of the bytes it
describes, and it is never the key of anything: nothing resolves
`digest` to bytes, and two blobs with identical chunk sequences are
still two blobs.

blob_hash.description: The whole-object digest of the blob this manifest describes.

digest.description:
The manifest's OWN content address, so a destination can verify it
received the manifest the source has. It names the manifest. It is
not an alias for the blob, it does not appear in `blobs`, and
nothing may resolve it to bytes (ADR-0034).

It covers the blob hash, the chunker parameters and the chunk
digests **in index order**, which is what makes it detect a
reordered manifest at all.

algorithm.description: The chunker that produced it, e.g. `fastcdc`. Stored rather than assumed: a manifest computed under another algorithm describes the same bytes and shares none of the same boundaries.

params.description: The chunker settings, on the wire for the same reason `algorithm` is. A destination whose defaults have moved has to be able to tell that what it was handed is not comparable with what it would compute.

avg.description: Target average chunk size in bytes; a power of two.

covered_size.description: The end offset of the last chunk. A manifest is internally consistent without being complete for a given blob; comparing this against the blob's size is the caller's question to ask.

chunk_count.description: How many chunks `chunks` carries. A destination that receives a different number has a truncated response rather than a tampered manifest, and the two are reported differently.

generated_at.description: When the source produced this manifest, in UTC.

chunks.description:
The chunk **sequence**, in index order. Not a set: the order is the
data, because a set of individually valid chunks assembled in the
wrong order is a set of valid chunks and the wrong file, and the
per-chunk digests cannot see it.

An empty array is valid and is what an empty blob has.

offset.description: Where this chunk starts in the blob. Carried even though it is derivable from the preceding lengths, because a receiver that recomputed it could not see a gap — it would have just filled it in.

length.description: How many bytes this chunk covers. Never zero.

digest.description: The BLAKE3 digest of this chunk's bytes. It is a place to fetch bytes from, never an identity for a blob.

served_by.description: The answering node's own peer id, so a destination can tell which end of the fabric replied. It is the only field about anything other than the manifest, and it is about the SOURCE — there is no field describing the caller, because the source formed no opinion about the caller.

CatalogSnapshot.description:
One snapshot payload: metadata, rows, and — for an incremental refresh
— the complete id set of each covered table.

**Why an incremental payload carries every id.** Deletion. A payload of
"rows that changed since T" says nothing about rows that stopped
existing, and a snapshot that silently keeps a deleted work forever is
not fresh, it is haunted. Shipping every id is cheaper than tombstones
in the control plane and has a property they do not: an incremental
refresh and a full rebuild of the same catalogue state converge on
identical contents.

blobs.description:
Byte identities and their shape (§13, ADR-0005) — never the bytes.
Those are the CAS's, and the peer already holds them in full (§80).

ids.description:
The complete id set per covered table, present only on an
incremental payload. A full payload does not need it: its rows ARE
the complete set.

An ABSENT set and an EMPTY one mean opposite things here — keep
everything, keep nothing — so the peer refuses an incremental
payload that omits a table rather than guessing.

watermark.description:
The high-water mark the NEXT incremental refresh asks from. A
separate field from `generated_at` because the source selects rows
AT OR AFTER it: re-sending a row costs one redundant upsert, while
excluding one that changed in the same instant costs a snapshot
that is silently missing it.

PeerIdentity.description:
The identity the answering node derived from the client certificate on
the connection, plus which node answered.

Every field here is the SERVER's conclusion. A caller cannot influence
any of it, which is the property that makes this endpoint worth having:
comparing `peer_id` against the id enrolment returned is an assertion
that pinning happened, and a 200 alone is not.

peer_id.description: The caller's membership id, as this node resolved it.

name.description: The caller's name in this node's membership records.

public_key.description:
The pinned key, so a caller can compare it against the one it
enrolled. The public half, as everywhere else in this API.

served_by.description: The answering node's own peer id.

speaks.description:
What the ANSWERING node's peer surface will actually do, so a
caller can tell a piece peer from a web seed before asking either
of them for anything (§27, ADR-0042).

`blob-content` is the ranged content route every serving node has
had since M4-09 — the byte channel a web seed is. `piece-exchange`
is the availability and piece routes; its ABSENCE is what makes a
member a web seed.

Derived from what the answering server was built with rather than
from what was configured, so it cannot claim a capability whose
routes refuse. A reader that meets a name it does not know must
ignore it, and one that meets a missing name must not conclude the
peer is broken — this list grows.

PeerReachback.description: Whether the answering node can reach the caller (#186, ADR-0040).

result.description:
`reachable` — something answered at `target`, whatever it answered.
`unreachable` — an attempt was made and nothing answered.
`unknown` — no attempt was made, because this node holds no
endpoint for the caller or serves no prober. A caller must not read
`unknown` as a fault: it is the absence of evidence, and refusing
an enrolment on it would refuse every peer that is simply off.

target.description:
The address this node tried, read out of its own membership record
