for the caller. Empty when no attempt was made. A caller learns
from it whether the address recorded for it here is still its own.

detail.description: A human-readable explanation, empty when reachable.

PeerAttachRequest.description:
What a Full Peer declares when it attaches. `peer_id` is a declaration,
not a credential: the controller compares it against the identity the
certificate proved and refuses a mismatch (ADR-0033).

peer_id.description: The membership id this peer believes it holds.

PeerAttachment.description:
A peer's attachment to a controller, as the controller records it.

Every field is the controller's conclusion, derived from the client
certificate. Nothing a caller sent is echoed back — including the
declared `peer_id`, which is compared and then discarded.

peer_id.description: The acting peer, derived from the certificate.

name.description: The acting peer's name in the controller's membership records.

public_key.description: The pinned key, as the controller holds it.

controller.description: The answering controller's own peer id.

control_plane.description:
A Full Peer runs no control plane of its own (ADR-0029). Stated in
the response so a peer that ever receives something else fails
loudly rather than assuming.

principal.description:
The kind of credential that was accepted. Never `admin`: a peer
certificate authorises the peer surface, acting as that peer, and
a peer reading `admin` here would have found a privilege
escalation (ADR-0033).

InventoryEntry.description: One blob, as the reporting peer's disk has it.

blob_hash.description: The canonical digest. Identity is the hash and nothing else (ADR-0005).

state.description:
A subset of `replicas.state` on purpose. `pending` is a
controller-side fact — a transfer it scheduled and is waiting for —
and a peer reporting it would be asserting something about the
controller's plans rather than about its own disk.

`corrupt` is a quarantined blob: bytes the peer still HAS and
cannot serve (ADR-0018). It is reported rather than omitted,
because omitting it reports the blob as gone and invites a
replacement transfer over the evidence, while reporting it present
leaves the controller believing in a copy nothing can read.

bytes_present.description: How many bytes the peer holds. 0 for anything not `present`.

verified_at.description:
When this peer last confirmed the bytes hash to their own name, if
it ever has. Absent rather than "now" when the peer has no
verification record: collecting an inventory reads a directory, it
does not re-hash a library, and stamping the collection time here
would manufacture verification evidence out of a directory listing.

A report that carries no `verified_at` never CLEARS the one the
controller already holds.

InventoryReport.description: What a peer sends the controller about its own store.

peer_id.description:
A DECLARATION, not a credential. The controller derives the acting
peer from the client certificate, compares this against it, and
refuses a mismatch (ADR-0033).

mode.description:
What this report asserts about a blob it does not mention: a full
report asserts absence, an incremental report asserts nothing.

observed_at.description:
When the PEER looked at its disk, on the peer's clock. The gap
between this and the controller's receipt is how stale the report
already was when it arrived.

entries.description:
The inventory. A full report with no entries is a peer that holds
nothing — a legitimate and important thing to be able to say, and
an implementation that read the empty set as "nothing to report"
would let a wiped peer keep its replicas forever.

InventoryOutcome.description:
What folding one report into `replicas` did. Counts, not rows: the
per-blob facts are durable in `replicas`, which is where anything
wanting the detail must look.

report_id.description: The receipt row this report was recorded as.

peer_id.description:
The peer the CONTROLLER acted on, derived from the certificate. A
peer comparing it against what it sent is asserting that its report
landed under its own identity.

changed.description: Existing rows whose state or byte count changed, excluding those moved to `missing`.

removed.description:
Rows this report moved to `missing`, by an explicit `missing` entry
or by absence from a full report. Counted apart from `changed`
because it is the only direction that makes the library less safe.

unknown.description:
Entries naming a blob this controller has no row for. Not an error:
a peer restored from a newer catalog legitimately holds bytes this
controller has not learned about, and there is no `blobs` row to
reference.

PeerRegistration.description:
What an operator asserts about another node.

There is deliberately no variant of this shape without `public_key`. A
registration carrying only a name and an endpoint would be a request to
trust whatever answers at that address — trust on first use — and
ADR-0012 pins keys rather than addresses.

endpoint.description:
Where to reach the peer. NOT its identity: posting the same
`public_key` with a different endpoint moves the peer, and its
`id`, its `enrolled_at` and everything referring to it are
unaffected.

Given as an origin — `https://host:port` — or as a bare
`host:port`, which is normalised to `https://host:port`: the
inter-peer path is mutually authenticated TLS (ADR-0012), so there
is exactly one scheme to guess, and `http://` is refused rather
than upgraded. A `unix:///path/to.sock` socket is accepted for a
peer on this host. Anything nothing could dial — no host, a port
that is not a port, an unknown scheme, a path where an origin
belongs — is a `400`, refused here rather than by whatever first
tries to dial it. The stored value is the normalised one: what
`GET /api/v1/peers` returns can be posted straight back.

Omitted or empty is legitimate and means "not known yet": a peer
may be enrolled by its key before anyone knows where it will live.

public_key.description:
Who the peer is — the exact string the other site's
`heyarr peers list` prints. This is the pin ADR-0012 describes, and
it is the only trust root in the inter-peer path.

Replica.description:
One peer's holding of one blob (§8) — what the CONTROLLER believes,
cached from what the holding peer last reported about its own disk
(M4-07).

verified_at.description: When these bytes were last re-hashed and matched their own name.

reported_at.description:
When the holding peer last confirmed this row in an inventory
report — null if no peer ever has.

Distinct from `verified_at`, and the difference is the point: a
peer can afford to confirm it still holds a blob far more often
than it can afford to read it, so the two decay at different rates.
A row nobody has confirmed recently is a fact about the past
whatever its `state` says, and garbage collection reads this before
deleting what it believes is a surplus copy.

IdentityUser.description:
A pinned user identity (§40, ADR-0048): the trust root a device's
enrolment cert is verified against. Carries no secret and no cert — the
pin is the public key.

recovery_encryption_key.description: The identity's X25519 recovery encryption PUBLIC key, `x25519:<hex>` (§41), registered when the user was pinned — the recipient new personal-state spaces are wrapped for. A public recipient only; the paper recovery secret never enters the server. Absent when none.

IdentityDevice.description:
A device key a user has vouched for (§40, ADR-0048, ADR-0068). The
admitting op token is deliberately absent: authentication evaluates
the presented op against the identity's op log rather than trusting a
stored copy. Its provenance is present: who admitted the device, and
which op.

encryption_key.description:
The device's X25519 encryption key, `x25519:<hex>`, when its
admission bound one — the recipient a space key is wrapped for
(ADR-0049), and what `heyarr device revoke` re-keys away from.

admitted_by.description:
The signer of the device's admitting op: the identity's genesis key
(`ed25519:<hex>`, equal to the user's key) for a cert-era or
first-device admission, or the key of the member device that
admitted it (ADR-0068). Empty only for a row whose op no longer parses.

admitting_op.description: The hash (`sha256:<hex>`) of the admitting op.

expires_at.description: The admitting op's expiry, for listing and pruning.

revoked_at.description:
Set once revoked — by the admin (`DELETE`), or by a member's remove
op the evaluation honoured; the row is kept so a re-presented op is refused.

media.description:
The external media toolchain THIS node resolved (ADR-0023). FFmpeg
is optional: a node without it still scans, ingests and serves byte
ranges, but probe and remux jobs stay pending until a worker that
has it claims them.

In a split-process deployment this describes the node answering the
request, not the fleet — the worker that would claim a probe job may
be another machine. `/api/v1/jobs` showing pending probes is the
other half of that picture.

guest.description:
Whether anonymous read-only browse (ADR-0074) is available on this
node. A client boots into Guest by reading the API with no
credential; this reports whether that is enabled.

DriftStatus.description:
The outcome of one comparison.

`unknown` means the comparison could not be MADE — nothing to compare
against, or a version string that is not a version. It is distinct from
`current` on purpose, and nothing may treat the two as equivalent: "we
could not tell" reported as "fine" is the failure this object exists to
stop.

`ahead` is not good news. For the schema it is the state in which an
older binary writes plausible rows against constraints a newer schema
depends on (§49); for the build it usually means the expectation is the
stale half.

`mismatch` means the two builds are known to differ with no ordering
between them — the same version tag built from different source, or two
commits with no semantic version on either side. Different, distance
unknown; never `current`.

BuildIdentity.description: A build — what it calls itself, and what it was built from.

BuildDrift.description:
How far the running build is from the expected one.

At most one of the three distance fields is non-zero: the most
significant semantic version component that differs. A distance spread
across three numbers is one nobody can threshold, so `v1.4.2` expected
against `v1.0.9` running reports one minor version behind rather than
claiming to be four minors and minus seven patches behind. All three are
zero unless `status` is `behind`.

detail.description:
Why a status is what it is, in a few words — chiefly why an
`unknown` could not compare. For a human; nothing should branch on
it.

SchemaDrift.description:
How many migrations separate this binary from its database.

A count rather than a flag, because seven unapplied migrations and one
are not the same operational problem: one is routine and the other wants
a backup taken before it runs. At most one of the two counts is
non-zero.

expected.description: The highest migration the comparison expects to exist.

applied.description:
The migration version actually applied to this database. Zero is
legitimate — a database that has never been migrated — and is
reported as behind by the full distance.

DriftReport.description:
Both drift checks, side by side and never merged.

They drift independently and they fail differently. A binary that is
current with its migrations unapplied is not a mild case of being behind
— it is a build running against a schema it was never tested on — and
reducing both to one "up to date" flag would let a current binary hide
an un-migrated database.

EventsInfo.description:
Where the event log currently is, so a client can follow the stream
from *now* rather than replaying from sequence zero.

head.description:
The most recent sequence number, and a resume point: pass it as
`?after=` on `/api/v1/events` to receive everything from here. An
empty log reports 0, which is already what "everything" means.

ok.description:
False when the head could not be read, in which case `head` is
meaningless. It is reported rather than 500ing because 0 is a
legitimate head, so a client cannot otherwise tell "nothing has
happened" from "we could not find out".

path.description: Where it was found. Absent when unavailable.

version.description: What it reported, e.g. `7.0.2`. Absent when unavailable.

detail.description:
Why an unavailable tool is unavailable, in a few words — "not found
on PATH", "did not report a version". Absent when available.

container.description:
ffprobe's `format_name` verbatim — a comma-separated list of every
name the demuxer answers to, e.g. `mov,mp4,m4a,3gp,3g2,mj2`. Kept
whole rather than reduced to one name, because which of those a
file "is" is a question with no answer, and the planner matches by
membership.

bitrate_bps.description: Null when the container declared none — a Matroska file legitimately has none.

bytes_read.description: What crossed the wire to answer this. §29's evidence.

materialised.description:
True when Range probing did not work and the whole blob was copied
(§29's fallback). Counted rather than silent: a fallback nobody can
see becomes the default without anyone noticing.

Publication.description:
An asset that is one of §69's four containers, with what its own
manifest declared.

page_count.description:
Page images in a comic archive. **Absent when unread**, which is not
the same as zero: an empty comic is a zero-page comic, and a PDF is
a publication whose length Heyarr has not counted. Reading a PDF's
page tree needs a PDF parser, and §69 says Heyarr does not render.

chapter_count.description:
Spine items in an EPUB — its reading order, which is the closest
thing an EPUB has to a length and is deliberately not called a page
count. Absent when unread.

content_url.description:
The ordinary blob endpoint. Named here so the single-endpoint
contract is visible in the response rather than only in ADR-0013.

verb.description:
Optional. Derived from the probe when omitted — watching when there
is video, listening when there is not. Derived from the probe
rather than the extension because a `.mkv` holding only audio is a
legitimate thing, and calling it "watching" puts it in the wrong
row of every continue-watching list.

content_url.description:
The ordinary blob endpoint (ADR-0013), on the peer routing selected
(§32) — **never the controller**, which stays out of the content
data path. Absolute when the source is another peer, so the client
connects to that peer directly; relative when the source is this
node, which is the origin the client is already talking to
(ADR-0029).

Bounded by the credential below, which expires. It is deliberately
NOT scoped to one blob: per-blob scoping is a grant (§77) and §54's
lease shape is the real answer, arriving in M7 alongside degraded
authorisation. Revisit when the first peer class arrives whose
access is a strict subset of the canonical set (§6, §19) — the same
trigger ADR-0030 records.

token.description:
A short-lived `read` credential for that URL. **Not scoped to one
blob** — see the endpoint description.

device_id.description:
A registered device. Required unless `client` is given; when both
are given the device's profile decides and `client` decides the leg.

client.description:
What the caller can decode (ADR-0069). Present, the answer carries
the leg — `mode`, `url`, `mime`, `reason`, `source` — and
`device_id` may be omitted.

ClientCapabilities.description:
A client's decoders, in ffprobe's codec vocabulary (`h264`, `hevc`,
`av1`, `vp9`, `aac`, `ac3`, `eac3`, `opus`, `mp3`, `mp2`) and the
ordinary container names (`mp4`, `mkv`, `webm`, `avi`). A client that
declares nothing at all is handed the bytes.

max_height.description: The tallest picture the client will take. Zero or absent means no limit.

PlaybackSource.description: What the probe found — the first video and audio stream.

reasons.description:
Why the decision is not DIRECT, or why nothing can be played. Empty
for a clean DIRECT.

peer_id.description: The replica chosen to serve from. Absent when unplayable.

remote.description:
The chosen replica is at another site. §31 prefers a local one, so
an instance where this is usually true is one where replication is
not working.

**The unproven note this carried is retired (M4-11, M4-14).** It
said nothing had ever run against a second peer; one exists now, and
§32's source selection routes against it — the same client with and
without a local replica is routed two different ways, and the
cross-site answer records that it fell back.

Read `routing` rather than this flag when you want to know why. This
is the planner's own summary of the source it was handed; `routing`
is the decision, with the peers it rejected and the reason for each.

content_url.description:
Where the bytes are, for a DIRECT plan — on the peer `routing`
selected, not on the controller. **Absent otherwise** — a REMUX or
TRANSCODE plan has no bytes to point at yet, and offering the
original would invite the client to play exactly what the plan just
said it cannot.

routing.description:
Which peer this read was routed to, and why not the others (§32).
Present on every plan **including a refusal** — especially on a
refusal. "Unavailable" with nothing after it cannot tell a peer that
is down from a peer that never had the bytes, and those have
different fixes.

mode.description:
The leg, present only when the request carried `client`
(ADR-0069). `direct` — fetch `url`, the ordinary blob endpoint.
`stream` — fetch `url`, the on-the-fly repackage. `unplayable` —
nothing holds the bytes.

url.description:
What to fetch for `mode`: `/api/v1/blobs/{hash}/content` for
direct, `/api/v1/playback/stream/{token}` for stream. Relative,
like `content_url`; for a direct plan on another peer it is
absolute on that peer.

mime.description: `video/mp4` for a stream; the asset's declared type for direct.

reason.description:
One sentence saying why the mode is not a clean direct — e.g.
`audio ac3 not decodable by client`, `container avi not playable
by client; audio mp2 not decodable by client`, `video 2160p
exceeds client max_height 1080 (transcoding video)`. Empty for a
clean direct. The same facts are in `reasons` as stable codes.

source.description: What the probe found, when anything has probed the bytes.

RoutingDecision.description:
The controller's source selection (§31, §32).

§32 lists six inputs. Three are implemented — site locality,
availability, health — and three are not: latency and bandwidth need
measurement infrastructure that does not exist, and transcode
capability is #112's unbuilt fleet advertisement. So this is an
**ordered preference that reports its reasons**, not a score with three
terms stubbed: same-site first, then this node, with latency appending
an element when it arrives rather than forcing every coefficient to be
re-decided at once.

peer_id.description: The selected source. **Absent when routing refused.**

reason.description: Why that peer won. Absent when routing refused.

rejected.description:
Every peer considered and not selected, each with **every** reason
it was not. A peer that is both unreachable and holds a corrupt
replica has two problems, and naming one of them produces a second
question after the first fix does not help.

code.description:
Stable. An operator's runbook and a client's branch both key on it.

`site_local` and `cross_site_fallback` are selections; the rest are
rejections. `site_local_preferred` and `another_source_chosen` are
rejections **with no fault in them** — the peer was eligible and
lost the ordered preference, which is how an operator sees that the
fallback existed before it was needed.

detail.description: Prose for a human. May change.

code.description: Stable. Clients branch on this, and a client branching on prose breaks when the prose improves.

detail.description: Prose for a human. May change.

ConsumptionSession.description:
One consumption of one asset by one device — watching, listening or
reading (§67, ADR-0024).

progress.description:
**Absent** until something has been recorded — not a zero locator.
Position zero is a real position, and a client cannot tell "at the
very beginning" from "never played" if both render as 0.

started_at.description:
When the session first played. Null for one created and abandoned,
which is what makes "nobody watched this" distinguishable from
"someone watched two minutes".

ended_at.description: When it reached a terminal state.

SessionProgress.description:
Where a session reached, as a **locator and a unit** — never a bare
number. A page number is not a number of seconds, and storing both as
"position" makes every reader guess which it has.

locator.description:
A decimal offset for `seconds`, a decimal page number for `page`,
or an `epubcfi(...)` expression for `cfi`. A CFI is opaque to
Heyarr, which stores and serves publications and never renders
them (§69).

progress.description: Recorded with the transition. Usually sent with `progress`.

search_id.description:
Groups these as the one search's answers they are. A different id
from a previous read means a search has happened in between and
this is a different set, not an update of the same one.

selected.description:
The provider's id for the chosen release. **Absent when nothing was
acceptable** — and note that is not simply the first of
`candidates`, which when everything was rejected is merely the
least bad.

candidate_id.description:
The **provider's** identity for the release, and what you name in a
`select`. The storage row's own id is deliberately not on the wire:
it identifies a row a re-search replaces, and a client holding one
would be holding a handle to something that vanishes.

accepted.description: Every gate held. A candidate that is not accepted is never acquired.

score.description:
The sum of the preferences that landed. Meaningful only among
accepted candidates: a rejected one's score is a number about
something that will not be used.

terminal.description: Meets every terminal condition, so the upgrade workflow would stop here (§62).

overridden.description: A person chose this against the ranking (§60's manual override).

override_detail.description: What the scorer had chosen instead, and what each scored.

reasons.description:
Every rule that was considered, not only the ones that failed — a
rule that ran silently is a rule nobody can confirm ran.

rejected_by.description: The gates that rejected this candidate. Absent when accepted.

state.description: §64's derived name, so this response stands alone.

UpgradeEligibility.description:
Whether this want could be **improved** (§60) — a different question
from either satisfaction axis. A want can be fully satisfied and still
improvable, and that gap is the whole upgrade workflow:

| state | meaning |
|---|---|
| not accepted | `MISSING`, keep searching — an *acquisition*, not an upgrade |
| accepted, not terminal | satisfied **and** still improvable |
| terminal | done; there is nothing left to want |

eligible.description: Nothing about this want's state rules an upgrade out.

status.description:
**Why** — an enumerated reason rather than a bare boolean, because
"no upgrade" has four completely different meanings and an operator
asking "why is this not upgrading" needs to know which.

`not_monitored` outranks `terminal`: a want that is both reports
the operator's decision, because "you told me to stop" is the more
useful answer than "it happens to be perfect".

`no_better_candidate` is the **normal** answer for a healthy
library — eligible, with nothing better found. It is what an
eligible want reports when nothing is on offer.

satisfied_by.description:
The asset that satisfies — the **best** one, by the same ranking
the search uses, so "what am I watching" and "what would I have
acquired" cannot disagree.

assets.description:
Every asset considered, with its full §63 reasons. An asset that
exists and was rejected appears here **with the rule that rejected
it**, which is the whole point of this endpoint.

satisfaction.description:
`not_applicable` is for ADR-0020's `linked` assets, which have no
blob and therefore nothing to replicate. Calling that `satisfied`
would be vacuously true and a lie by construction.

missing.description:
The peers that should hold the bytes and do not. `converging` with
no list of what is missing is a status nobody can act on.

unproven.description:
**Whether this answer is true by construction rather than by
replication having worked.** Computed per response from the Full
Peer target set: `true` when that set is this node alone, `false`
when it names two or more peers.

On a single-peer deployment placement is satisfied the moment
content is, because there is nowhere for bytes to converge to, and
`converging` is unreachable — so a client must not read `satisfied`
there as evidence that replication works. On a two-peer deployment
the axis is answering a real question and this is `false`.

It was hard-coded `true` while one peer was the only deployment
that existed. It did not become `false` when the second peer
arrived: a Heyarr on one machine is a supported configuration
forever, and a constant `false` would be a lie on every one of
them.

It is a response field rather than only a note in this document
because a caveat the reader of the response never sees is a caveat
that does not work.

id.description:
Absent makes this a notification, which is answered with `202` and
no body rather than a result.

params.description:
For `tools/call`: `{ "name": "...", "arguments": { ... } }`. The
argument shape for each tool is its `inputSchema` from `tools/list`,
and unknown fields are refused rather than ignored — an agent that
misspelled one finds out instead of getting a cheerful empty result.

result.description:
For `tools/call`, MCP's content envelope: a `content` array with a
text block every client can render, plus `structuredContent`
carrying the same value as JSON. Both, so an agent gets prose it can
quote **and** a shape it can branch on rather than having to parse
the prose.

code.description:
JSON-RPC 2.0 codes, plus one. `-32700` parse error, `-32600` invalid
request, `-32601` method or tool not found, `-32602` invalid params,
`-32603` internal error, and **`-32001` forbidden** — outside the
reserved range because a refused scope is not a malformed request,
and an agent that cannot tell "you may not do this" from "you asked
wrongly" will retry the wrong one forever.

data.description:
The actionable half. A refused scope names the tool and the scope it
needs; a deferred §71 verb names the milestone that brings it.

id.description:
Stable for a given release from a given provider, and the ranking's
tie-break — so it must not be a position in a response. Two
candidates sharing an id is a `400`, because it would make the
ranking depend on the order they were sent in.

title.description:
What the indexer called it. **Never parsed** — attributes are
extracted by the provider, and re-deriving them from the title at
scoring time would be a second, invisible extraction.

attributes.description:
What could be determined about the release, keyed by attribute
name. A key that is **absent** (or explicitly `null`) means "could
not be determined", which is different from a zero value and is
reported as `undetermined` rather than as a failure.

A provider that cannot tell must leave the attribute out. HDR
detection in Milestone 2 is a substring match on the ffprobe
profile and is a recorded weakness; a release *title* is worse
evidence, not better.

selected.description:
The candidate that would be acquired. **Absent when none was
acceptable** — and note this is not simply the first of `ranked`,
which when everything was rejected is merely the least bad.

accepted.description:
Whether every gate held. A candidate that is not accepted is never
acquired, whatever it scored.

score.description:
The sum of the preferences that landed. Meaningful only among
accepted candidates: a rejected one's score is not a near miss, it
is a number about something that will not be used.

terminal.description:
This candidate meets **every** terminal condition, so the upgrade
workflow has nothing left to want (§62).

A profile with no terminal rules is **never** terminal — vacuous
truth over an empty set would turn "never stop looking" into "stop
immediately". A rejected candidate is never terminal either.

reasons.description: Every rule that was considered, in the profile's own order.

rejected_by.description: The gates that rejected this candidate. Absent when accepted.

rule.description:
The rule's machine-readable identity, `<attribute>.<op>`. Clients
branch on this; a client branching on prose is one that breaks when
the prose improves.

score.description: The contribution, present only for preferences that landed.

detail.description: The prose half, for a human.

DesiredItem.description:
"This content should exist under these conditions" (§55) — the row that
makes Heyarr more than a catalogue.

It anchors to a **Work**, the semantic entity (§11), which exists
whether or not any bytes do. Never to an Asset: an Asset is a file that
exists by definition, and wanting a file you already have is not a
coherent thing to say.

scope.description:
How much of the work is wanted — the whole thing, or one edition of
it (a season, a particular release, a language).

**There is no `episode` scope, and that is a limitation rather than
an omission.** §11 makes the *series* the Work and an edition the
season, so an episode is an Asset — a file that exists — and there
is no entity anywhere for an episode nobody has yet. Knowing which
episodes *should* exist is what a metadata provider is for, and
that is deferred out of Milestone 3.

What this costs today, stated rather than papered over: with no
metadata provider, content satisfaction for a series-scoped want is
"an acceptable asset exists", **not** "every episode exists". A
want for a series is not a completeness guarantee in this
milestone.

work_id.description: Always set, even at edition scope.

edition_id.description: Present only at edition scope — absent, not null, at work scope.

monitor.description:
"Keep looking for something better", which is **not** the same as
wanting (§60 keeps both words). An unmonitored want that is
satisfied is finished, terminal profile or not: the operator said
"get me this", not "keep improving this". Running the upgrade
workflow over unmonitored items is how *arr installations
re-download libraries nobody asked them to touch.

reason.description:
Free text, never interpreted. It exists because a library
accumulates wants and six months later nobody remembers why one is
there.

AcquisitionState.description:
Where a want has got to (§64).

§64 draws twelve boxes in a single column — `MISSING`, `SEARCHING`,
`CANDIDATES_FOUND`, `SELECTED`, `QUEUED`, `DOWNLOADING`, `VERIFYING`,
`INGESTING`, `AVAILABLE`, `CONTENT_SATISFIED`, `PLACEMENT_CONVERGING`,
`FULLY_SATISFIED` — but they are **not twelve steps along one road**.
They are a presentation of four independent facts, and this object
carries all four alongside the name.

Showing only `state` would reintroduce at the edge exactly the collapse
the storage model exists to prevent: a client that can see
`CONTENT_SATISFIED` but not which of §56's two questions was answered
cannot tell "we have it" from "we have it everywhere".

state.description: §64's name, **derived** from the fields below and never stored.

phase.description:
Where the acquisition pipeline is.

There is deliberately **no `missing` or `available` phase**. Both of
§64's names mean "nothing in flight" and differ only in whether
Heyarr holds bytes — so with them as phases, a fruitless upgrade
search returns to `MISSING` and reports a perfectly good library as
empty.

managed.description:
Whether Heyarr holds bytes for this want. Independent of `phase`,
because a want can be acquiring an **upgrade** while already
holding a good copy.

content.description:
"Do we hold bytes the quality profile accepts?" (§56)

`unknown` is distinct from `not_satisfied`: "nobody has looked" and
"we looked and the answer is no" lead to different actions, and
collapsing them makes a fresh want indistinguishable from one just
found wanting.

There is no `converging` here — no partial file half-satisfies a
profile.

placement.description:
"Are those bytes on every Full Peer that should hold them?" (§56)

`not_applicable` is for ADR-0020's `linked` assets, which have no
blob and therefore nothing to replicate. Calling that `satisfied`
would be vacuously true and a lie by construction: `FULLY_SATISFIED`
would then mean "one copy, on one disk, with no integrity
guarantee".

`converging` is reachable and observed as of Milestone 4: a
two-peer deployment moving real bytes reports it mid-transfer and
`satisfied` once the transfer lands.

On a deployment whose Full Peer target set is this node alone it is
still `satisfied` the moment content is — there is nowhere for bytes
to converge to. `GET /api/v1/desired/{id}/satisfaction` reports that
case as `placement.unproven: true`; this listing does not, so read
the satisfaction endpoint before treating `satisfied` here as
evidence that replication works.

detail.description: Why the last pipeline move happened, when it was a failure.

bytes_total.description:
Total bytes of the transfer in flight, as the download client last
reported it. Omitted when there is no transfer; zero when the client
has not said the size yet.

bytes_done.description:
Bytes fetched so far of the transfer in flight, refreshed on every
download poll. With `bytes_total`, this is how far a download has
got — omitted when there is no transfer.

CreateDesired.description:
Name the work by `work_id` **or** `work`, and the profile by
`quality_profile_id` **or** `quality_profile`. Supplying both of a pair
is a `400` rather than a silent precedence rule.

edition_id.description: Required at edition scope, refused at work scope.

quality_profile.description: The profile's name, for when a person is typing this.

WorkDescriptor.description:
Content named semantically, whether or not it exists. Resolved through
the same `(content_type, work_key)` get-or-create the scanner uses, so
wanting something and later scanning it converge on one Work.

year.description:
Optional, and part of the identity when present. A year in the
title (`"Blade Runner (1982)"`) is understood too; an explicit year
wins, because the caller said so.

UpdateDesired.description: An omitted field is left alone. The target cannot be changed.

FollowSourceRequest.description:
The intent behind `POST /followed-sources`. Source-agnostic (#396): give
a feed identity (a `url` or a `tvdb_id`) and a series identity (a
`work_id`, or a `title`); the type is inferred. Exactly one of `work_id`
and `title`. A quality profile is required — every projected episode is
measured against it.

url.description: A feed identity to infer the source from — a TVDB series URL in Phase 1.

tvdb_id.description: A numeric TVDB series id, as an alternative to url.

work_id.description: An existing series work. Give this or title, never both.

title.description:
The series title, for a series not yet catalogued. Get-or-creates the
series work the same way `want_content` does.

quality_profile.description: The profile by name, as a person would say it. Give this or quality_profile_id.

monitor.description: Keep looking for a better copy of each episode. Defaults to true.

backfill.description:
How much back-catalogue to pull on the first poll. `from_now` (the
default) archives only episodes airing after you follow; `full` walks
the whole back-catalogue into wants.

want_subtitles.description:
Languages (ISO-639-1 codes) to want a subtitle in for every projected
episode (ADR-0085). Each poll projects a subtitle want per language;
the fetch driver acquires each once the episode's video is held. Empty
wants none.

retention.description: Reserved. Phase 1 keeps everything; a non-empty value is refused.

FollowedSource.description:
A followed source as the API presents it — the subscription plus the
derived counts and health a caller reads to answer "is this working".

title.description:
The followed work's human name, inlined so a list of subscriptions
reads as titles rather than as work ids a client must join against
`/works` (#430). Empty when the work is gone.

type.description: The inferred source type. Reported, never a request field.

feed_ref.description: The source-stable handle the feed adapter polls — a TVDB series id.

want_subtitles.description: Languages this source projects a subtitle want for (ADR-0085); omitted when none.

items_known.description: How many items the feed has yielded.

items_archived.description: How many of those are held at the profile.

health.description:
The state of the feed adapter this source is polled through. `unknown`
means none is configured, or none has been checked yet.

FollowedItem.description:
One Item a followed source's feed yielded (ADR-0056), with what heyarr
did about it.

edition_id.description:
The grouping the item belongs to — a season, for a series. Absent
for a source type that has none.

item_key.description:
The source-stable identity the feed adapter supplied — an "S02E05",
a podcast GUID, a video id. It dedupes the item across polls and is
this listing's sort key.

published_at.description:
When the source said it emitted the item. Absent when the source did
not say — a real and distinct answer from any particular instant.

attributes.description: Per-item, per-type facts (a season/episode number, a duration).

want.description:
The item-scoped want this source projected, or null when it has
projected none.

archived.description:
heyarr holds bytes for this item that satisfy the source's profile.
Derived from the want's content axis, so a client need not know
§64's vocabulary to render a tick.

FollowedItemWant.description: The projected want's id and §64's three axes.

SearchResult.description: What `POST /search` returns (ADR-0075). Neither list is ever null.

EpisodeHit.description:
A part of a work that matched by its own title (ADR-0075): `edition` is
an episode a series scan produced, carrying its file; `item` is an entry
a followed source projected (ADR-0056), which has no file of its own.

primary_asset.description: Present on an `edition` hit that holds bytes the caller may see.

ContinueEntry.description: One card of the continue rail (ADR-0075).

attributes.description: The edition's per-type facts — season and episode, for a series.

asset.description:
The asset the session is on. For a session on a blob-less (linked)
asset only `asset_id` and `edition_id` are set.

WorkSummary.description:
One work a content-intent search returned, with its per-type attributes
and its poster (ADR-0075) — what a result row draws.

tvdb_id.description:
The work's stored TVDB external id (ADR-0050), when it has one — the
feed identity `follow_source` takes as `tvdb_id`, so a client can
follow a search result in ONE step rather than by a title that might
create a second work (decision 2, M12). Omitted for a work with no
stored tvdb id; the client then asks the operator for one. This
surfaces an id already in the library — not a live TVDB discovery
search for series the library does not yet hold.

DiscoveryResult.description:
One candidate work a discovery search returned (#451) — a work that may
NOT be in the library yet, resolved live from the metadata provider.

type.description:
The followed source type this candidate would be followed as
(`tv_series` today), so a client picks the right follow flow without
inferring it from the id's shape.

tvdb_id.description:
The candidate's TVDB series id — the value `POST /followed-sources`
takes as `tvdb_id`, so a client follows a discovery result in ONE
step. Present for a `tv_series` candidate.

overview.description: A short human description when the provider supplied one.

SessionView.description: A caller's own identity and effective authority (ADR-0061).

kind.description:
How the caller authenticated: `session` (web-login/QR, ADR-0053),
`device` (device cert, ADR-0048), `service` (a bearer token), or
`anonymous` (authentication disabled on a loopback listener).

principal_id.description: The identity the caller acts as ("ed25519:<hex>" for a user); empty for the anonymous identity.

device_key.description: The approving/authenticated device key for a session or device caller — the value an operator names to grant management. Absent otherwise.

scopes.description: The effective authority this credential carries.

can_write.description: Whether `scopes` admits write — i.e. whether follow/unfollow will succeed for this caller as it stands.

management_authorized.description:
True when this is a session whose approving device holds a
follow-management grant (ADR-0061) — the reason a session can write.
False for a read-only session and for a service token (whose write
authority, when it has it, is its own scope, not a grant).

ManagementGrant.description: One device authorised to manage followed sources from a web-login session (ADR-0061).

reason.description: A free-text operator note; may be empty.

ManagementGrantRequest.description: The operator's consent that a device may manage followed sources (ADR-0061).

device_key.description: The approving device key to authorise, as GET /session reports it for that device ("ed25519:<hex>").

reason.description: A free-text operator note ("the operator's phone"). Optional.

capabilities.description:
What this node can therefore do, as a set — and therefore which
jobs it can claim.

Stated rather than left for a client to derive, because deriving it
means knowing that a **disabled** provider contributes nothing, and
a dashboard that got that wrong would report "indexing available"
for a provider somebody switched off.

Empty is a legitimate answer, not an error: it is exactly what
ADR-0025 describes.

capability.description:
Echoes the `?capability=` filter, so a client holding a response
knows which question it answers.

holders.description:
Every **live** advertisement, one entry per worker. An expired one
is absent rather than present-and-stale: showing it with a "last
seen" column would invite an operator to route work to a machine
that is switched off.

Empty is a legitimate answer. A fleet where nothing has advertised
yet, and a fleet whose workers can do nothing anybody routes on, are
both supported configurations (ADR-0023).

available.description:
The union across the fleet: every capability at least one live
worker holds, sorted.

Stated rather than left for a client to derive, because deriving it
means knowing that an expired holder contributes nothing — and a
dashboard that got that wrong would offer a transcode nothing can
run.

worker_id.description:
The advertising worker. It is the same string that appears as a
job's lease owner, so a stuck job and a fleet entry name the same
thing. Unique per process: a restarted worker advertises under a new
id and its predecessor's advertisement expires.

peer_id.description: The node this worker runs on, which is the unit the question is asked about.

expires_at.description:
When this advertisement stops being honoured unless the worker
renews it. Present so an operator can tell a worker that is about to
fall out of the fleet from one that has just arrived.

name.description:
The exact string a job's `required_capability` is matched against.
Dotted and hierarchical — `ffmpeg`, `ffmpeg.encoder.hevc`,
`ffmpeg.encoder.av1.vaapi` — and matched by equality, never by
prefix.

source.description:
How this was established, which is what says whether it is
re-verified.

| source | means | re-verified |
|---|---|---|
| `binary` | a tool resolved at startup (ADR-0023) | no — installing ffmpeg under a running Heyarr is not a supported flow |
| `probe` | the capability was **exercised**: a real encode of a handful of frames to a null sink | yes, on a beat, and the advertisement narrows when it stops passing |
| `service` | an external network service is configured (ADR-0025) | no; its reachability is `/api/v1/providers`' answer |

detail.description: A few words for an operator — which encoder proved it.

proved_at.description:
When the proof was taken, **not** when the row was written. The
difference matters: a re-advertisement that reused a cached proof
would otherwise look freshly verified.

name.description:
The operator's name for this provider, unique within an instance.
It is what appears in routing, in health, and in a release
candidate's `provider` field — so it is the operator's word rather
than a generated identifier.

capabilities.description:
What this provider can do for us.

**Empty when the provider is disabled in configuration.** That is
how "configured and switched off" is distinguished from "not
configured at all": the first appears here with nothing it can do,
the second does not appear.

`metadata` is declared and nothing implements it in this milestone
— §84's list does not include metadata providers. It exists so that
the first one is a change to configuration rather than a change to
the registry.

healthy.description: Whether the last check found the provider usable.

detail.description:
What was observed, in a few words. A status with no reason is one
nobody can act on, so this is always present.

version.description:
The API version the service reported.

This is what replaces version **pinning** for a service Heyarr does
not install (ADR-0026): not controlling the version does not mean
ignoring it. A version outside the supported range is reported
unhealthy naming both numbers, and is **never** a startup failure.

checked_at.description:
When the last check ran. **Absent means never checked**, which is
distinct from `healthy: false`.

QualityProfile.description:
A quality profile (§62). It says three different **kinds** of thing,
not three degrees of one:

| section | meaning |
|---|---|
| `accept` | a **gate**. Fail one and the candidate is rejected outright, whatever else it offers. |
| `prefer` | a **score**. Never a gate — a candidate meeting no preference at all is still acceptable, merely worse. |
| `terminal` | a **stop condition**. The point at which the upgrade workflow has nothing left to want. |

Collapsing any two produces the *arr behaviour §61 rejects: a
preference that silently rejects, or an upgrade loop with no ceiling
that never terminates because "better" is unbounded.

An **empty `terminal` and an absent one are the same thing** — "there
is no condition under which this profile is finished", which is legal
and means *never stop looking*. The seeded `archival` profile is
exactly that.

name.description: Unique. This is what a DesiredItem names (§55).

prefer.description: Scored. None is required; each contributes its weight.

terminal.description:
Stop conditions. **All** must hold for a candidate to be terminal.
Empty means this profile is never finished.

seeded.description:
Came from Heyarr's defaults rather than from an operator. Seeding
converges on the name and never overwrites, so an edited default
stays edited — this is how you can tell you are looking at one.

WriteQualityProfile.description:
On `POST`, an omitted section is empty. On `PUT`, an omitted section is
**left alone** and a section sent as `[]` is **cleared**.

QualityRule.description:
One assertion about a release: an attribute, a comparison and an
operand. The same shape serves all three sections — what differs is
what a failure *means*, and that belongs to the section rather than to
the rule. One rule type is what lets §63 report all three the same way.

The attribute vocabulary is **closed**, so a rule can be validated when
it is written rather than when it is evaluated. Adding an attribute is
a code change, which is correct: something has to know how to extract
it from a release, and an attribute nothing populates is a rule that
silently never matches.

attribute.description:
`resolution` is vertical lines (480, 720, 1080, 2160) rather than a
label, because "4K", "2160p" and "UHD" are three spellings of one
number.

`source` is **not ordered**, even though there is an obvious
quality ordering among `remux`, `bluray`, `web-dl` and the rest. An
ordering here would be a second scoring system living outside
`prefer`, invisible to §63's reasons — the opaque scoring §61
rejects. Say "bluray beats webrip" with two preferences instead,
and it appears in the explanation.

op.description:
`gte` and `lte` are numbers only; `in` and `nin` are names only. A
comparison that does not apply to the attribute's type is a `400`,
as is a list operand with `eq` — which would otherwise validate and
then silently match nothing.

value.description:
A bare JSON value whose shape follows the attribute: a whole number,
a name, a list of names (for `in`/`nin`), or a boolean. The kind is
read from the JSON and then checked against the attribute, never
coerced — so `"1080"` against `resolution` is a caught typo rather
than a working rule.

weight.description:
The score contribution, meaningful **only** in `prefer`. May be
negative — a penalty is a real thing to want. May not be zero: a
preference that cannot affect the score is indistinguishable from
an absent one, and keeping it means an operator believes something
is being preferred when nothing is.

A weight on an `accept` or `terminal` rule is a `400`, not an
ignored field. It is the mistake this design most invites, and
silently dropping it would leave an operator believing a gate is
scoring.

Device.description: A registered device and the capabilities it declares (§68).

device_key.description:
The client's own stable identifier, and the idempotency key for
registration. Not a credential and never checked as one.

last_seen_at.description:
When this device last registered. The only thing that makes a stale
row identifiable later.

DeviceProfile.description:
What a device says it can play. A zero maximum means **no limit
stated**, which is deliberately different from a limit of zero: a
client that omits `max_bitrate_bps` is not claiming it can play
nothing.
